full_judgment:
Md Imman Ali J : This Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal arises out of the judgment and order dated 23-2-2011 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 4310 of 2010 disposing of the Rule, with observations and a direction upon the parties to strictly follow the terms and conditions of the solenama filed in the Family Suits.

2. The facts relevant for disposal of the instant petition, in brief, are that the petitioner Anika Ali and the respondent Rezwanul Ahsan were married on 23-12-2002 under Muslim Law and the dowry was fixed at Taka 10,00,000 of which 2,00,000 was shown as paid, although, according to the petitioner, no money was paid. A child Farzan Ahsan, was born during their wedlock on 24-12-2003. Soon thereafter, the relationship between the petitioner and the respondent deteriorated. The petitioner claims that she was physically and mentally tortured by the respondent who was a drug addict from the time of his studies in America and he had been arrested on several occasions due to his drug addiction and he had also received treatment for his addiction in New Delhi as well as in Bangladesh. However, all this information was suppressed at the time of the marriage. It is alleged by the petitioner that in July, 2004 the respondent pushed her out of his house during the night after torturing her, but she went back to the house of the respondent for the sake of her son. On 26-7-2004 the respondent again pushed the petitioner out of his house. However, there was reconciliation on the assurance by the respondent, in the presence of the guardians of both the parties, to the effect that he would not take, drugs again and would not physically and mentally torture the petitioner and would arrange to rent separate accommodation. On 10-11-2004, they lived together in the rented accommodation, but the respondent again physically tortured the petitioner on 17-12-2004 and pushed her out of his house and compelled her to divorce him by the power given to her in the Kabinnama and accordingly the petitioner divorced the respondent on 18-12-2004. The petitioner then filed Family Suit No.175 of 2005 before the Court of 2nd Assistant Judge and Family Court, Dhaka against the respondent for her dower money and maintenance for herself and her minor son. The suit was transferred to the Court of 5th Additional Assistant Judge and Family Court, Dhaka where it was renumbered as Family Suit No. 322 of 2005. In her suit, petitioner detailed the matters narrated above. She claimed that the respondent did not pay any maintenance to the petitioner since 26-7-2004 and therefore, claimed for herself maintenance at the rate of Taka 20,000 per month from 26-7-2004 to 18-12-2004, i.e Taka 1,00,000 In addition she claimed Taka 60,000 for her maintenance during the three month's iddat period. She claimed maintenance for her minor son at the rate of Taka 15,000 per month from 26-7-2004 to 30-6-2005, i.e Taka 1,65,000 .

3. The respondent filed Family Suit No. 284 of 2005 before the Court of 2nd Assist-ant Judge and Family Court, Dhaka for custody of his minor child. On transfer to the Court of 5th Additional Assistant Judge and Family Court, Dhaka the suit was renumbered as Family Suit No. 484 of 2005. The respondent claimed, inter alia, that after the wedding both families were quite happy, but when his wife became pregnant she and her parents were not happy. After their son was born, he was under the care of his (the respondent's) mother when his wife went abroad to study on two occasions. The minor child was all along under the care of his father (the respondent). He took out an education insurance policy and a general insurance policy in his sons name for Taka 9,00,000 respectively. The child's paternal grand-mother took out an insurance policy for Taka 15,00,000 in which the child was named as the beneficiary. The respondent further claimed in his plaint that at one stage his wife insisted that he take a separate rented house, and when he declined to do so, she left with their child, taking with her all her jewelry and clothes. When he requested to her to return, she stated that she would not cohabit with the respondent unless they lived in a separate house. She also claimed the remainder of her dower money. Thereafter, he rented a flat in Banani, but his wife (the petitioner) refused to rejoin him unless he paid up the dower money. On 10-11-2004, with the help of his father, the respondent paid up the dower money and his wife joined him in their rented flat along with child on 10-11-2004 However, his wife started argument with him without any good cause and eventually left his house on 17-12-2004 without his permission taking with her their child as well as jewelry and other material belongings. Thereafter, she sent him her divorce on 18-12-2004. The respondent further claimed in his plaint that his ex-wife left the child with her mother while roaming around. He also came to know that she had gone abroad leaving the child with her mother. Claiming that the child is not safe in that house and was not receiving proper care and attention, the respondent prayed for an order of custody and full care and control over the child.

4. Family Suit No. 322 of 2005 filed by the petitioner and Family Suit No. 484 of 2005 filed by the respondent proceeded simultaneously and the instant petitioner's lawyer advised her to settle the matter amicably. On 3-4-2006 two solenama were executed, one for each of the suits. The solenama in Family Suit No. 322 of 2005 provided inter alia that the dower money of Taka 8,00,000 will be paid by the respondent in twelve installments, a cheque for Taka 66,666 was paid to the petitioner on 3-4-2006 and eleven post dated cheque would be handed over to the petitioner on that date; a cheque for Taka 60,000 was paid to the petitioner on 3-4-2006 as maintenance for the period of iddat; maintenance for the minor child was fixed at Taka 15,000 per month from January, 2005; the child would visit his father on two days per week from 10-00 AM to 10-00 PM till his admission in school and after his admission in school, from 10-00 AM to 8 PM on Fridays and from 5-00 PM to 8-00 PM on any one weekday during school term.

5. The solenama executed in Family Suit No. 484 of 2005 provided maintenance for the child at the rate of Taka 15,000 per month from January 2005 which may be increased in the future upon consultation between the parties and would be deposited in the account of the petitioner with HSBC Bank. The due amount of Taka 2,25,000 for the months January, 2005 to March, 2006 would be adjusted with the current month's payment ;the minor child would visit his father on two days per week from 10-00 am to 10-00 PM before admission in school and after admission in school the visit would take place from 10-00 AM to 8-00 PM on Fridays and 5-00 PM to 8-00 PM on any one school day during the week. The child would be admitted to school after discussion amongst the parties and the petitioner (mother) would be entitled to take her minor son abroad subject to permission of the Court.

6. According to the petitioner the respondent did not comply with the terms and conditions of the solenama and as a result she filed violation Miscellaneous Case No. 893 of 2007 (Arising out of Family Suit No. 322 of 2005) before the Court of 5th Additional Assist-ant Judge and Family Court Dhaka which is still pending. On the other hand, the respondent filed an application for enforcement of the decree on 13-11-2007 which was rejected by the Family Court on 26-11-2008 upon hearing the parties and the respondent, without preferring any Appeal against the said order dated 26-11-2008, filed a Writ Petition being No. 2890 of 2009 in the form of habeas corpus, claiming that the child was in unlawful custody of the petitioner. By judgment and order dated 12-8-2009 the Rule in that Writ petition was discharged with the observation that if the Writ-petitioner files any petition for enforcement of the terms of the solenama before the lower Court the Court concerned shall dispose of such application within 2(two) months from the date of filing thereof. The respondent thereafter filed Family execution Case No. 77 of 2009 before the Court of 5th Additional Assistant Judge and Family Court, Dhaka for execution of the judgment and decree dated 11-7-2007 passed in Family Suit No. 484 of 2005. The petitioner filed an application for dismissing the execution case on the ground that an earlier application for enforcement of the decree on 13-11-2007 was rejected on 26-11-2008 and respondent did not prefer any Appeal against that order and also that the execution case was barred by limitation (since the judgment and decree was dated 3-4-2006, decree signed on 9-4-2006). By his order dated 14-1-2010 the learned Assistant Judge, 5th Additional Assistant Judge Court, Dhaka rejected the instant petitioner's application for dismissing the execution case. The instant petitioner challenged the said order of dismissal by way of Family Appeal No. 30 of 2010 before the Court of learned District Judge, which upon transfer to the learned Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka was dismissed by judgment and order dated 22-6-2010. The instant petitioner then challenged the dismissal of the Appeal by preferring Civil Revision No. 4310 of 2010 before the High Court Division. By the impugned judgment and order dated 23-2-2011 the Rule was disposed of with direction upon the parties "to strictly follow the terms and conditions of the solenama and violation of any term of the solenama by any party shall be treated as contempt of Court. The petitioner is further directed to receive the entire dues within 14 days now deposited with the Court and the opposite party is also directed to regularly pay the maintenance cost of the child born during their wedlock and the petitioner is also directed to make available the child before his father the opposite party, twice in a week as per the term of the aforesaid solenama."

7. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and order dated 23-2-2011 passed by a single Bench of the High Court Division the petitioner has filed the instant Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal.

8. Mr. Md Asaduzzaman, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submits that the learned Judge of the High Court Division committed a gross illegality by effectively acting as the executing Court by directing the petitioner to receive the money paid into Court and also directing the parties to follow the terms and conditions of the solenama and violation of any terms of the solenama by any party shall be treated as contempt of Court. He submits that such finding direction and observation is illegal, unwarranted and is liable to be set aside. He submits that the High Court Division failed to appreciate that the execution case was barred by limitation under section 16(3) of the Family Court Ordinance, 1985, and by the impugned judgment and order, the decree has effectively been executed, although it was barred by limitation. He further submits that even if the decree is not considered to be a money decree, it is still barred by limitation under Article 182 of the Limitation Act, read with section 16(3C) of the Family Court Ordinance, 1985. He submits that the High Court Division has committed an illegality in entertaining the Family Execution Case.

9. Mr. AF Hasan Ariff, learned Senior Counsel appearing for the respondent, submitted that the petitioner has not been prejudiced in any way by the impugned judgment and order. He further submits that in a case of this nature where the marriage has broken down between two adults, the child of the union is the victim, and his best interests should be protected.

<u>10. We have considered the submissions of the learned advocates for the petitioner and the respondent and perused the judgment and order of the High Court Division as well as those of the Courts below. We note that both the parties to the marriage filed Suits in the Family Courts with their own claims and narrated events that led to the dissolution of the marriage. Both the family, suits were heard simultaneously and decreed in terms of a solenama filed in each of the family suits. The terms and conditions in each of the solenama are essentially the same. The parties have agreed to the amount of dower money, maintenance for the wife and maintenance for the child. They also agreed, though by implication, that the child, who was at that time about two years and three months old, should remain in the custody of his mother and a schedule of access/ visits was agreed upon whereby before his admission in school the child would visit his father's house on two days in every week between 10-00 AM. After the child's admission in school he would visit his father's house only on Fridays between 10-00 AM and 4-00 PM on one school-day per week between 5-00 PM and 4-00 PM. In this way the dower, maintenance and custody of access to the child was mutually agreed upon by the parties. 'It was also agreed' that the mother of the child could take him abroad subject to the permission of the Court. The family suits were decreed on 3-4-2006. The respondent filed an application for enforcement of the solenama, which was rejected on 26-11-2008. For non-performance of the terms of the solenama, the petitioner filed a violation Case, which is still pending.</u>

11. As the mother of the child took him out of the country and the father could not see his child and allegedly did not know his whereabouts, and in view of the fact that the mother of the child had married another person, he filed Writ Petition No. 2898 of 2009 in the form of a Writ of habeas corpus. The High Court Division upon hearing both the parties by judgment and order dated 12-8-2009 discharged the Rule upon finding that since the minor boy way staying with his mother as per order of the Court, it could not be said that the boy was illegally detained. It was observed that since in the solenama it has been categorically written that the mother of the child shall send him to his father's house on two days every week, the Writ-petitioner (respondent herein) is not without remedy and that he could take proper steps for enforcement of the terms of the solenama. The Writ Bench directed as follows: "If the petitioner files any such petition before the lower Courts for enforcement of the terms of the solenama, the Court concerned shall disposed of such application, if any within 2(two) months from the date of filing thereof." Accordingly, the respondent, father of the child, filed the Family Execution Case No. 77 of 2009 which has culminated in the judgment and order impugned before us.

<u>12. Since both the parties to the ill-fated marriage amicably agreed to abide by certain terms and conditions with regard to the payment of dower, maintenance and custody of the child, as embodied in the solenama, we do not find any illegality in the essence of the impugned judgment and order. Effectively, the High Court Division has ensured payment of the money due to the petitioner. Since the payment of maintenance for the child a continuous process, the door of the Courts is always open to the child's mother to ensure the payment of the maintenance for the child, if ever there is any default in payment. Equally, the father has the right of access as mentioned in the solenama.</u>

<u>13. With regard to the custody of the child, against is a matter that can be redressed by the Family Court, should here by any default in implementing the Court's order. Moreover, the order in relation to custody of a child should never be presumed to be inscribed in stone. Matter such as custody must always remain fluid since charge in circumstances at any time require the terms of the custody of the child to be varied upon a fresh application in order to comply with the age-old principle that the welfare of the child is a paramount consideration and in modern parlance "the best interests of the child" must be given due consideration.</u>

14. Mr. Hasan Ariff appearing for the respondent candidly submitted that the child of the broken marriage finds himself as the victim and his best interests must be ensured. The child of the marriage Farzan Ahsan is now almost seven and half years old. Although, under Mohammedan Law, hizanat (custody) of a male child over the age of seven years usually goes to the father, there are numerous decisions of our apex Court that it the welfare of the child demands, then the custody may be retained by the mother of the child. There is nothing to preclude either parent of the child from filing fresh application before the appropriate Court for changing the terms relating to the custody/access of the child.

<u>15. We may also mention that within the modern concept of custody and other matters concerning children, there is a requirement that the child should be allowed to express his views. (see Article 12 of the Convention of the Rights of the Child (CRC) quoted below). This is a small progression from section 17(3) of the Guardians and Wards Act 1890, which provides that if the minor is old enough to form an intelligent preference, the Court may consider that preference. The Court when considering any matters relating to the custody of the child should also keep in mind the provision of Article 3 of the CRC, which provides that in all actions concerning children, whether undertaken by public or private social welfare institutions, Courts of law, administrative authorities of legislative bodies, the best interests of the child shall be a primary consideration. Article 12 of the CRC provides as follows:—</u>

<u>Article 12.1: States parties, shall assure to the child who is capable of forming his or own views the right to express those views freely in all matters affecting the child, the views of the child being given due weight in accordance with the age and maturity of the child.</u>

<u>2. For this purpose, the child shall in particular be provided the opportunity to be heard in any judicial and administrative proceedings affecting the child, either directly, or through a representative or an appropriate body, in a manner consistent with the procedural rules of national law. In has been held by this Division in a number of cases that the views of the minor child is of no value (see Abdul Majid Sarker vs State, 55 DLR (AD) 1 and Badiur Rahman Chowdhury vs Nazrul Islam, 16 BLD (AD) 263. However, those cases relate to a different category of minors, i.e. those deciding to leave the paternal home in favour of their paramours. There is a marked divergence in the views of the Appellate Division in case of custody of children who are victims of a broken marriage. A clear distinction may, therefore, be made in case of children who find themselves victims of turbulent or broken-down marriages. The decision as to which parent shall have the custody of the child and how much access may be afforded to either parent is a most delicate one. A wrong decision may create a traumatic situation for the child, which would result in indelible psychological damage throughout his/her life. In this context it would be wise to allow the child to freely express his/her views so that the judge adjudicating upon the matter can decide what the welfare or the best interest of the child demands. The final decision, of course, lies with the judge, who will come to a decision upon consideration of all the attending facts and circumstances. These aspects have been elaborately discussed in the case of. Abdul Jalil vs Sharon Laily Begum Jalil, 50 DLR (AD) 55, Their Lordships agreed that "nothing is more paramount, not even the rights of the parties under the rules of personal law or statutory provisions, than the welfare of the children which must be the determining factor in deciding the question of custody of children whether in a proceeding in the nature of habeas corpus or in a proceeding for guardianship under the Guardians and Wards Act 1890." Their Lordships also made reference to Abu Baker Siddique vs SMA Baker, 38 DLR (AD) 106, where it was held that "If circumstances existed which justified the deprivation of a party of the custody of his child to whose custody he was entitled under Muslim Law, Courts did not hesitate to do so." In this case the eight year old child was also asked about his preference, and such preference was taken into consideration by the trial Court before giving custody to the mother. The matters to be considered before deciding the issue of custody of children were also elaborately discussed in this case.</u>

16. Hence, at any time in the future either of the parents of the child shall be at liberty to move the appropriate Court for an appropriate order in respect of the custody of/access to the child in the light of prevailing circumstances at that time and the Court shall be at liberty to entertain such application and to pass necessary order in respect of the child's custody keeping in view the best interests of the child giving the child an opportunity to express his views. The Court should also keep in mind the provisions of Article 9 of the CRC Article 9(1)(2) and (3) provide as follows :

"9(1) States Parties shall ensure that a child shall not be separated from his or her parents against their will, except when competent authorities subject to judicial review determine, in accordance with applicable law and procedures, that such separation is necessary for the best interests of the child. Such determination may be necessary in a particular case such as one involving abuse or neglected of the child by the parents, or one where the parents are living separately and a decision must be made as to the child's place of residence.

(2) in any proceedings pursuant to paragraph 1 of the present article, all interested parties shall be given an opportunity to participate in the proceedings and make their views known.

(3) States Parties shall respect the right of the child who is separated from one or both parents to maintain personal relations and direct contact with both parents on a regular basis, except if it is contrary to the child's best interests.

<u>17. With regard to the applicability of provisions of international instruments, which have not been incorporated into our Municipal Law, reference may be made to the judgment of BB Roy Chowdhury, J in Hossain Muhammad Ershad vs State, 21 BLD (AD) 69. It may be noted that in the Abdul Jail case cited above reference was made to the Declaration of the Rights of the Child 1959. Unless provisions of international instruments are contrary to our domestic laws, the beneficial provisions may profitably be referred to and implemented in appropriate cases. (see State vs Metropolitan Police Commissioner, 60 DLR 660).</u>

<u>18. The observation of the learned Judge of the High Court Division that "violation of any terms of the solenama by any party shall be treated as contempt of Court," being unwarranted and beyond jurisdiction, is hereby expunged. Save as mentioned above, we do not find any reason to interfere with the judgment and order of the High Court Division. This petition is dismissed with the above observations without, however any order as to costs.</u>

End.

full_judgment:
Mr. Muhammad Abdul Mannan. J:-This Civil Revision arises out of the judgment and decree passed by the Subordinate Judge, Chandpur on 28.2.1985 in Title Appeal No. 14 of 1983 reversing those of the learned Munsif, 1st Court, Chandpur dated 29.12.82 in Title Suit No. 183 of 1977 sending back the suit on remand for hearing of the arguments of both sides and deliver a judgment on merit of the suit rejecting the solenama filed by the parties. The aforesaid judgment and decree was passed in terms of the compromise petition filed by defendant No. 1 and 2 the plaintiff No. 1. The defendant No. 2 as petitioner preferred this application before this Court. 

	2. The opposite parties 1-4 as plaintiffs filed the suit before the learned Munsif. Their case, in short, is that they entered into an agreement to purchase the land of defendant No. 1 on 11.8.76 on payment of consideration of Tk. 7,000/- of which they paid Tk. 6,500/- as earnest money and the plaintiffs were given delivery of possession of the suit land. But the defendant No. 1 did not execute and register the deed of kabala within time and so they were constrained to file the suit for specific performance of contract before the Court. 

	3. Defendant Nos. 1 and 2 filed joint written statement denying al materials allegations of the plaint. Their assertion is that the price of the suit land will be Tk. 25,000/- and it was impossible to enter into a contract of sale of the suit land at Tk. 7000/- and actually there was no contract of sale at all. Defendant No. 1 sold 36 decimals of land in plot No. 1018 by a kabala executed and registered on 17.3.1977 and delivered possession of the same to the purchaser. Defendant Nos. 2 and 3 possessed the land. 

	4. That the case was heard by the learned Munsif and the plaintiffs and the defendants adduced their evidence by their respective witnesses which concluded and the suit was placed for argument on 23.12.82 but on that date the defendants prayed for time and, date was shifted to 29.12.82. On 29.12.82 when the suit was called for arguments of the parties a compromise petition was filed defendant Nos. 1 and 2 and the plaintiff No. 1. The learned Munsif on hearing the compromise petition allowed the same and a decree was passed in terms of the com-promise petition on 29.12.82. 

	5. The plaintiffs being aggrieved preferred appeal before the learned District Judge, Chandpur which was heard by the learned Subordinate Judge, Chandpur on 28.2.85 and reversed the judgment and decree passed by the learned Munsif and sent back the suit on remand as stated above. 

	6. The defendant No. 2 as petitioner preferred this revisional application before this Court against the order of remand of the suit to the trial Court. 

	7. Mr. Abdus Salam Khan the learned advocate appearing for the petitioner submits that it is a consent decree and so the appeal before the lower appellate Court as well as the revision before this Court is not competent. 

	8. Section 96 clause 3 of the C.P.C. provides that no appeal shall lie from a decree passed by the Court with consent of the parties and in such circumstances fresh suit is to be filed for declaration that the decree is illegal, inoperative and the same is not binding upon the parties. He also submits that the learned appellate Court should have decided the case finally without sending the suit on remand under Section 99 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the learned Court also failed to show fraud, collusions mistake or misapprehension and misrepresentation on the part of the learned lawyer who conducted the compromise petition. He also submits that total claim of the specific performance of contract was satisfied by the compromise decree and in such circumstances the order passed by the lower appellate Court was illegal. 

	9. Mr. Syed Mohammad Hossain, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party Nos. 1-5 submits that the hearing of the suit was concluded except the arguments by the parties and the pleadings of the plaintiff was proved by P.W. 1, who is plaintiff No. 2 on behalf of all the plaintiffs of the suit including plaintiff No. 1 as tadbirker in this case for them. The plaintiff No. 1 did not come to the Court to depose any more but on the date fixed for arguments on 29.12.82 a compromise petition was initiated on behalf of defendant Nos. 1 and 2 with an alleged signature of plaintiff No. 1 and the learned lawyer of the plaintiffs without objection placed it before the Court. At the time of hearing of the petition he also did not fell to take evidence of plaintiff No. 1, the party to the compromise petition and the lawyer admitted that the suit was proved by the evidence of plaintiff No. 2 and so it would be sufficient for the purpose of the compromise petition. The learned lawyer acted illegally and malafide in collusion with the defendants without calling the plaintiff No. 2 who deposed as P. W. 1 in the suit to prove the pleadings of the plaintiffs in order to be definite about the contents of the compromise petition. 

	10. He submits that the compromise petition allegedly signed by plaintiff No. 1 on his own and on behalf of the rest plaintiffs and the acceptance of such a compromise petition and passing the judgment and decree in terms of the compromise petition by the learned Munsif amounts to arbitrary and illegal act. The learned-Advocate also submits when the fact of compromise is disputed the same cannot be taken with consent of the plaintiffs opposite parties and so section 96(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure will not be applicable in this suit. He also submits that the compromise, petition was filed with misrepresentation of facts of the entire suit so the same is not binding upon the opposite parties and the judgment and decree of the trial Court was not legally and properly passed after hearing the arguments of the plaintiff and the defendant and the same was not under order 20 rule 4 sub-rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure and so the order of remand by the lower appellate Court was passed legally. In support of aforesaid contention he refers A.I.R. 1952 Allahabad page 29 wherein it was held. 
"When the consent upon the basis of which a decree has been passed by the Court is itself challenged in the Court of appeal, it cannot be taken for granted that the decree was a consent decree. A consent decree must mean of decree validly consented to either by the party himself or by his duly authorised agent. If the question has to be decided and it cannot be prejudged by 
holding that because on the face of it there was a consent decree, no appeal lies to the appellate Court." It was further held, "That the words used in the power of attorney and wide enough to include the power not only of presenting a petition of a compromise signed by the parties themselves but also to enter into a compromise and to file the petition of compromise in Court." But the vokalatnama filed by the learned Advocate of the trial Court does not give the absolute power and authority of compromise and to file the petition without their signatures instead of filing by the plaintiffs themselves before the Court. 

	11. The learned Advocate also submits that the general power given by the party in the printed vokalatnama will not be sufficient to file any compromise petition without conSent and signature of the plaintiffs in the compromise petition. The power is given only for the purpose of con-ducting the case and filing of any petition genuinely and correctly signed by the par-ties whether they are plaintiffs or defendants. The learned Advocate also refers to 27 D.L.R. page 249 wherein it held by this Court that, "The authority to compromise is a vital authority which must to compromise is a vital authority which must be specifically given and cannot be implied or inferred. The petition for compromise ought to have been signed by all the appellants and specific power to compromise must be given by the executants to the Advocate concerned. In the absence of all these essential prerequisites the learned Advocate for the appellants had no authority to sign the compromise petition on behalf of the appellants even if the terms of compromise are in favour of the appellants. Similarly the com-promise petition by which the respondents are relinquishing their claim upheld by the Courts below to have been signed by all the respondents who were plaintiffs in the suit. The affidavits in support of petition may be sworn by any one of the appellants or any one of the respondents but the deponent must be specifically empowered by the parties concerned to affirm the affidavit on their behalf and the petition must also contain a statement to that effect. These requirements are essential and must be fulfilled to guard against any possible fraud". 

	12. The learned Advocate for the petitioner cited one decision reported in 42 DLR (AD) regarding consent decree where-in it was held that 
	"Plaintiffs elected to give up all the reliefs prayed for in the suit and to limit their prayer, by amendment, to a declaration that they are the sole legal heirs of the loanee. On understanding with the plaintiffs, the defendants neither opposed the amendment nor advanced any argument. Since the plaintiffs elected to relinquish all reliefs except the one for saving the suit from limitation and to secure some benefits for themselves, they are bound by the principle of estoppel and cannot be allowed to argue for the same reliefs which they had voluntarily abandoned. The decree obtained by them being based on understanding and consent of the parties, they are not permitted to take any appeal from such consent decree. On the principle the defendant is also barred from preferring any appeal from the High Court Division's judgment."

	13. I have heard the learned Advocate of both sides and perused the records, the documents and the rulings cited above. The rulings cited by the learned Advocate for the petitioner in 42 D.L.R. (AD) page 234. It is seen, the facts and circumstances of the case are distinguishable with the instant case. In the case referred in the decision, the parties with their own accord relinquished some of the reliefs they claimed in the suit as plaintiffs and accordingly the order was passed by the Court. But here in this suit the parties did not file this compromise petition with their signature but the same was filed allegedly by the plaintiff No. 1 on behalf of the plaintiff Nos. 2-4. This does not give absolute authority to the plaintiff No. 1 which is challenged by the plaintiff Nos. 2-4 and the pleadings of the suit was proved by P. W. 1 the plaintiff No. 2, for all the plaintiffs and same was adopted in passing the order on compromise. In such circumstances it is seen that no actual authority was given to the plaintiff No. 1 by the plaintiff Nos. 2-4 and also to the lawyer to prefer this compromise petition before the trial Court and accordingly it was a misrepresentation in the case and indicates some amounts of fraud on their part. So the same ruling will not be any help in this case. The suit was heard at length and the evidence was closed and only the arguments of both the parties were left out for a decision on merit of the suit. And all on a sudden on the date of arguments this compromise petition was filed allegedly by the parties before the Court and same was considered and accepted. I think the order passed by the learned Munsif was not proper and accordingly to law as he ought to have taken a due care to satisfy himself in delivering the judgment and decree on such compromise petition. I also think that the learned lower appellate Court can finally heard the case without sending the same to the trial Court because there was no argument, of the advocates in the trial Court but he could decide the suit on the basis of the evidence on record before him. The learned lower appellate Court sent the case on remand for arguments and to deliver judgment and pass decree after discussing the suit on merit. But this remand is not illegal as it is within the jurisdiction and competence of the lower appellate Court. Therefore, the learned lower appellate Court was justified in sending the case on remand to hear the arguments in the suit and then deliver the judgment on merit. 

	14. In the result, I discharge the Rule without any order as to costs.

	15. Let the lower Court's records of the case be sent down at once to the Court's below. 
	
	End.

full_judgment:
Mr. S.K. Sinha J.:- Heirs of defendant no. 1 after taking leave from this Court obtained this Rule from the judgment and order dated 20th March, 2008 of the learned District Judge, Dhaka in Civil Revision No. 93 of 2007 affirming that dated 12th March, 2007 of the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka in title suit no. 95 of 1982. 

2. Opposite parties no. 1 and 2 instituted Title Suit No. 95 of 1982 in the 1° Court of Joint District Judge, Dhaka for partition of the suit lands against the petitioners and others. The learned Joint District Judge by judgment and order dated 19th November, 2002 decreed the suit in preliminary form and allotted saham of .031/3 acres of land to the plaintiffs and 06120/170 acres of land to the defendant no.1. An Advocate Commissioner was appointed thereupon for allotment of the saham. The Advocate Commissioner submitted a report on 29th August, 2005. The report of the Advocate Commissioner was accepted and the final decree was drawn up on 30th November, 2005. Thereafter the petitioners filed an application under sections 151/152 of the Code of Civil Procedure for correction of the final decree on the ground that the final decree was drawn up not in conformity with the preliminary decree and that the Advocate Commissioner performed the commission beyond their knowledge and allotted lands to the plaintiffs from the lands in possession of the defendant no .1 wherein the heirs of the defendant no. 1 have their multistory building. The learned Joint District Judge upon hearing the parties rejected the said application the learned District Judge also maintained the said order. 

3. It is contended on behalf of the petitioners that the Courts below erred in law in maintaining the final decree despite the fact that the final decree has been drawn up not in conformity with preliminary decree. It is further contended that in the preliminary decree the learned Joint District Judge allotted saham to the parties with a direction that the saham should be allotted according to their possession but the Advocate Commissioner had allotted about one decimal of land from the saham of defendant no. 1 and that too, on demolition of the building and that the learned District judge erroneously accepted the said report without applying its judicial mind. 

4. Mr. Golam Mohiuddin, learned Advocate for the plaintiff-opposite parties, on the other hand, submits that the defendants have not filed any appeal against the final decree and therefore, they are not entitled to maintain an application for correction of the final decree under section 152 C.P.C. The learned Advocate contends that the defendant no.1 has encroached about one decimal of land from the total area of the land and accordingly, the Advocate Commissioner has allotted the plaintiffs' saham out of chita plot No.1 in accordance with the preliminary decree passed by the trial Court. 

5. In the application for correction of the final decree, the petitioners stated that the Advocate Commissioner though mentioned that he performed the commission work in presence of both the parties on 10' June, 2005 but in fact, he did not serve any notice upon them, inasmuch as, he executed the commission in presence of Moazammel Hossaina Chowdhury, Dr. Mozammel Hossain Chowdhury, Romani Kanta Ghosh, Advocate, Deb Kanta Ghosh, Advocate and Haji Amjad Hossain, who are plaintiffs representatives and their lawyers, from which, it was apparent that the Advocate Commissioner performed the commission work exparte. They further stated that the Advocate Commissioner allotted .0367 acres of land to the plaintiffs from Chita plot No. 1 in failing to consider that the defendant no. I (ga) by registered kabala dated 25' March, 2004 purchased .0480 acres of land out of the suit plot from Hoshneara Jahan Chowdhury but the Advocate Commissioner amaigamated the said lands of defendant no. 1 (ga) while allotting saham to the plaintiffs. 

6. The learned Joint District Judge rejected the application for amendment mainly on the reasoning’s that the defendants did not specifically mention the manner of correction and/or amendment of the final decree and that the application was vague and indefinite. The learned District Judge on the other hand, observed that the defendant petitioners did not file written objection against the Advocate Commissioner's report, that they prayed for amendment of the final decree after lapse of times and that, the trial Court had committed no error of law in rejecting the amendment of the final decree, inasmuch as, there was no clerical or arithmetical error in drawing up the final decree by the trial Court. 

7. The learned District Judge failed to notice the positive case of the defendants that the Advocate Commissioner secretly submitted the report and therefore, they had no knowledge about the report. Therefore, there was no scope for filing written objection against the Advocate Commissionaire's report inasmuch as, the Advocate Commissioner according to defendants, had performed the commission work secretly without serving any notice. 

8. The final decree was drawn up on 30" November, 2005 and as soon as they came to know about the final decree, which was drawn up not in conformity with the preliminary decree, the defendants-petitioners filed application for amendment of the final decree on 20' March, 2006. The learned Joint District Judge observed that the application for amendment was vague and indefinite, but the learned District Judge was of the view that as no objection was filed against the commissioner's report, the defendants-petitioners had no right to file application for amendment of the final report. Therefore, I find that both the Courts below rejected the application on two different grounds. The petitioners clearly mentioned in paragraph 7 of their written objection that the Advocate Commissioner allotted saham to the plaintiffs after amalgamating the lands purchased by defendant no. 1 (ga) from Hoshneara Jahan Chowdhury by registered kabala dated 25th March, 2004. Therefore, I find that the defendants have clearly mentioned the mistake that has been committed by the Advocate Commissioner. 

9. In the trial Court the plaintiffs claimed saham from the lands purchased by the defendant no. 1 on the ground that the plaintiffs gave money to him for purchasing lands. The trial Court turned down their Chaim observing as follows:" বাদীপক্ষ যৌথ অর্থে ও স্বার্থে উক্ত জমি অধুনামৃত ১নং বিবাদী খরিদ করিয়াছে মর্মে দাবী করিলেও যৌথ অর্থের উৎস ও স্বার্থ বিষয়ক কোন দালিলিক প্রমাণ আদালতের সম্মুখে আনিতে ব্যর্থ হইয়াছে।Accordingly the trial Court rejected the plaintiffs claim for allotment of saham of .0466 acres of land in the suit land and allotted only .032/3   acres of land out of the joint property. While passing the decree the trial Court clearly observed: ১নং বিবাদী অন্যান্য ক্রেতাদের সহিত নিজ নামে খরিদা জমি ব্যতীত বাদী ও অধুনামৃত ১নং বিবাদী কর্তৃক যৌথ নামে খরিদা সম্পত্তিতে হিস্যা অনুযায়ী ছাহাম পাইতে পারে। বর্ণিত আলোচনা মতে বাদীগণ একত্রে ০৩২/৩ একর বাবদ প্রথম একটি এবং বিবাদীগণ একত্রে ০৬১২০/১৭০ একর সম্পত্তি বাবদ প্রত্যেকের দখল অনুসারে একটি পৃথক ছাহাম পাইতে পারে। This observation clearly shows that the plaintiffs and the defendant will get their respective sahams without disturbing others respective possession. None of the parties has taken any exception from the judgment of the trial Court. The accepted the trial Court's judgment. 

10. The Advocate Commissioner in his report found the defendant has a one storey building but the plaintiffs plot is vacant. The trial Court clearly observed that while allotting saham the Advocate Commissioner shall maintain the respective possession of the parties. The Advocate commissioner did not say that the heirs of the defendant no. are in possession of excess lands their share. Therefore the question of encroachment of land does not wise. The heirs of defendant no.t claimed that the Advocate Commissioner in collusion with the plaintiffs amalgamated the defendant No.1(ga)'s land purchased from Hoshneara Jahan Chowdhury and allotted saham to the plaintiffs out of that land. In course of hearing of the rule, Mr. Golam Mohiuddin, learned Advocate for the plaintiffs has admitted that the Advocate Commissioner has allotted about one decimal of land from the defendants dwelling house. According to Mr. Mohiuddin, the defendants have encroached about one decimal of land from the plaintiffs share and constructed a building and that the defendants have constructed their house in excess of their lands allotted by the trial Court in their saham. The plaintiffs did not raise this point either in the trial Court or at any stage of the proceeding that after the preliminary decree, the defendants had encroached one decimal of land from the share of the plaintiffs. Mr. Mohiuddin argues that the defendants have encroached this land during the pendency of the suit but if the defendants have encroached such land the trial Court would have noticed the said fact. The trial Court clearly observed that the parties would get saham maintaining their respective possession. Therefore, the Advocate Commissioner cannot travel beyond the preliminary decree and from this admission of Mr. Mohiuddin, it is apparent that the Advocate Commissioner has allotted about one decimal of land from the lands of defendants possession where the defendants have their dwelling house. 

11. In paragraph 8 of the counter affidavit, the plaintiffs stated that the defendant petitioners had resisted the delivery of possession and accordingly, they prayed for deployment of one contingent of police force for affecting the delivery of possession. This statement also supports the defendants claim that plaintiffs are trying the take possession of one decimal of land by demolishing of the defendants building. In the preliminary decree no such direction was made by the trial Court to give saham to the plaintiffs after demolition of the defendants building. In that view of the matter, it is apparent that the final decree has been drawn up not inconformity with the preliminary decree. Now the question is that whether the court can amend and or rectify the final decree if decree is not inconformity with the preliminary decree. According to Mr. Mohiuddin, the Court cannot rectify the decree in the absence of an appeal being filed by the defendants from the final decree. The learned District Judge was also of the view that the Court has no power to correct the final decree other than accidental slip or omission that has been cropped up at the time of drawing up the final decree. 

12. From the statements of the plaintiffs and the report of the commissioner, there is no doubt that the final decree has been drawn up not in conformity with the preliminary decree and that the plaintiffs are trying to take possession of their saham from the share of the defendants by demolition of the existing building. The trial Court did not pass any such direction while passing the preliminary decree. In Bazidullah and others Vs. Sukumar Chandra Das, 1986 BLD (AD) 251, the Appellate Division on consideration of a decision of the Calcutta High Court and Privy Council observed as follows: 

"It is not necessary to multiply instances, when the various High Courts of India had taken uniform view that the Court can always amend the decree if there is a mistake that had crept in for bringing the degree in conformity with the judgment." 

Their Lordships also considered the case of C.K. Mukhopadhya Vs. S.M.S.B. Debi, AIR 1924 (Cal) 895. The Calcutta High Court took the view that the Court by taking resort to Section 152 C.P.C. can amend decree to conform to the judgment at any time and there is no time limit to such amendment. In this case, as observed above, the final decree was drawn up on 3015 November, 2005 and the application for amendment of the decree was filed on 20th March, 2006, as soon as the defendants came to know that the final decree was drawn up not inconformity with the preliminary decree. In that view of the matter, the Court is not powerless to correct and/or amend the decree if the said decree is apparently contrary to the preliminary decree. 

13. After the submission of the commissioner's report, the plaintiffs have come up with a new case of encroachment of one decimal of lands by the defendants from their saham, although they have not made such allegation at any stage of the proceedings. The trial Court also did not pass any such a direction to give saham to the plaintiffs out of the lands in possession of the defendants. In that view of the matter, the learned Joint District Judge without applying his judicial mind has drawn up the final decree in pursuance of the Advocate Commissioner's report which has been submitted not in conformity with the preliminary decree. This defect can be detected on the face of the record and in that view of the matter the Courts below have committed error of law in not amending the final decree. On consideration of the facts and circumstances of the matter. I find substance in the contention of the teamed Advocate for the petitioners that the Courts below on a superficial consideration of the Advocate commissioner's report rejected the defendants application for amendment of the final decree which has been apparently drawn up beyond the preliminary decree. Accordingly, I find substance in this rule. 

14. In the result, the rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The impugned judgments are set aside. The final decree is hereby set aside. The learned trial Court is directed to draw up a fresh final decree in accordance with the preliminary decree and in drawing up the final decree, if it feels necessary to appoint a fresh Advocate Commissioner at the cost of the founding parties for allotment of saham in accordance with the preliminary decree, it shall appoint an another Advocate commissioner. 

End.

full_judgment:
Mr. Borhan Uddin, J:- Supplementary affidavits do form part of the main application. At the instance of the petitioners leave was granted under Section 115(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure to decide the question of legality of the impugned order. 

2. The petitioner's case in short, is that the opposite party Nos.I-25 as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No.26 of 1991 for partition in the Court of Joint District Judge, 10 Court, Chandpur impleading the petitioners and opposite parties No.26-71 as defendants contending inter alia that the suit land belonged to Monir Uddin, Sonar Uddin and Muluk Jan who died leaving 4 sons namely Sadar Ali, Kofil, Sekandar and Fazar Ali. The Plaintiff Nos.l-1 I are heirs of the said Fazar Ali, plaintiff Nos.12- 16 are heirs of the Kofil Uddin, Plaintiff Nos.17-22 are heirs of the Safar Ali and plaintiff Nos.23-25 are heirs of Sekandar Ali. Muluk Jan died leaving her brother Gonortiddin. Said Gonoruddin died leaving defendant Nos.1-2 who transferred some of their shares to defendant Nos.3-4. The plaintiffs share in the suit land is 3/4 and rest are belongs to defendants. S.A. Khatian prepared wrongly. The plaintiffs claimed their sham but the defendants refused to their claim and hence the present suit. 

3. Defendant Nos. t and 2 and defendant Nos.3-34 contested the suit by filing separate written statements but during pre-emptory hearing predecessor of the defendant petitioners being died they failed to adduce evidence in the suit. Suit was decreed. Preliminary decree was drawn on 01.01.2003. Having learnt  about the judgment and decree, the defendant petitioners filed Miscellaneous Case No.41 of 2003 under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the Court of learned Joint District Judge, 90 Court, Chandpur. 

4. Upon contested hearing the learned Judge rejected the application vide order No.169 dated 15.04.2004 holding that since final decree is not drawn up as yet, the petitioners can seek saham in the partition suit which is Still in the form of preliminary decree and there is scope to amend or alter the saham of the parties allotted by the preliminary decree. 

5. Relied the order dated 15.04.2004, the defendant petitioners without preferring appeal against the order, filed an application in the Court of learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Chandpur under Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure praying their saham, in the suit land and the said application was accepted by the court on 10.05.2004 but subsequently when the opposite parties filed written objection, the learned Judge upon hearing the parties, rejected the application by his order dated 12.3.2006. 

6. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the order, the defendant petitioners preferred Civil Revision No.10 of 2006 in the Court of learned District Judge, Chandpur under Section 115(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure. After hearing the parties, the learned District Judge rejected the civil revision by his judgment and order dated 22.04.2008 and thereby affirmed the order of the trial court. 

7. In the said backdrop the defendant petitioners moved this Revisional application under Section 115(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the present Leave. 

8. Mr. S. N. Goswami, the learned advocate appearing for the petitioners submits that the appellate court below committed an error of law in passing the impugned order without considering the legal aspect that until final decree is drawn up, in a partition suit the court may direct adjustment or allotment or decide other incidental matters. The learned Advocate also submits that the appellate court below committed an error of law in not holding that the court can make a supplementary preliminary decree in respect of such additional Joint properties as the parties may be compelled to discover in pursuance of the order. The learned Advocate also submits that the appellate court below failed to appreciate that in a partition suit, if the defendants asked for partition of their shares, more than one preliminary decree can be drawn up and thus committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. In support of his submissions the learned Advocate referred to the case of 
Jadunath Roy and others Vs. Parameswar Mullick and others, reported in AIR 1940 PC 11; the case of Phoolchand and another Vs. Gopal Lal, reported in AIR 1967 (SC) 1470; the case of Abdul Ali Bhuian' Vs. Jahura Khatun & others, reported in II MLR (AD) 143, the case of Moolchand and others Vs. Deputy Director, consolidation and others, reported in AIR 1995 SC 2493 and the case of Ghulam Hossain and others Vs. Khan Mohammad and others, reported in Pakistan Law Reports (Vol. VII), Lahore, 776. 

9. Mr. Naim Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite party Nos.1-5 and 7-27 by filing a counter affidavit in support of the impugned judgment and order submits that though the defendant-petitioners filed written statement but did not contest the suit and as such their claim could not be determined in the partition suit for want of evidence. In elaborating his submission the learned Advocate submits that the preliminary decree passed in the partition suit does not contain any declaration as to the rights of defendants because the defendants though filed a written statement but did not contest the suit by adducing oral or documentary evidence and as such their application for suborn is not maintainable till the preliminary decree is modified declaring their share in an appeal of the said decree. The learned Advocate also submits that the petitioner s did not prefer any Miscellaneous Appeal against the order passed in the miscellaneous case filed under Order 9 Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In support of his submission, the learned Advocate referred to the case of Sarbeswar Panda and others Vs. Bibhabasu Panda, reported ire AIR 1977 Calcutta, 288; the case of Venkata Vs. Pethi Reddy, reported in AIR 1963 (SC) 992; and also the case of Smt Parvathamma Vs. A. Muniyappa and others, reported in AIR 1997 (SC) 370. 

10. Heard the teamed Advocate at length perused the Revisional application and the annexure annexed thereto, Supplementary Affidavit filed by the petitioners, counter affidavit filed by the opposite parties and the decisions referred by the learned Advocates of the parties. 

11. I have carefully gone through the judgment and order passed by the courts below. Admittedly, the defendant-petitioners filed a written statement in the suit for partition but subsequently they did not contest the suit by adducing any oral or documentary evidence. However, after preliminary decree was drawn up they filed Miscellaneous Case No.41 of 2003 under Order 9 Rule 13 of the. Code of Civil Procedure. The said miscellaneous case was rejected by the learned Joint District Judge, Court, Chandpur, with the following findings:
“মূল মোকদ্দমা অদ্যাবধি চুড়ান্ত ডিক্রি না হওয়ায় অত্র প্রার্থী পক্ষের মূল মোকদ্দমার প্রাথমিক ডিক্রি বহাল রেখে ছাহাম চাওয়ার সুযোগ রয়েছে। এ ছাড়া প্রাথমিক ডিক্রিমূলে পক্ষদের বরাদ্দকৃত অংশ পরিবতর্ন সংশোধনের সুযোগ রয়েচে। কাজেই মূল মোকদ্দমার Contesting রায় ডিক্রির ফলে অত্র প্রার্থী পক্ষের ক্ষতির কোন কারণ আছে মর্মে প্রতিয়মান হয় না।” 

12. The petitioners without preferring appeal against the order filed an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the court of Joint District Judge, Court Chandpur, which decreed the suit, praying for their saham. The application was accepted by the court but after filing of the written objection by the plaintiff-opposite parties, the trial court, upon hearing the parties, rejected the application holding that: 
"এক্ষেত্রে ছাহাম প্রার্থী বিবাদীদের অত্র দরখাস্ত বিবেচনার কোন সুযোগ নাই কারণ বন্টনের মত অবশিষ্ট জমি নাই, তদুপরি ২৮-১১-২০০২ ইং তারিখের রায় মূলে নালিশী জমি Adjust  হওয়ায় অত্র ছাহাম প্রার্থী বিবাদিদের দরখাস্ত কোন ভাবেই বিবেচনার সুযোগ না থাকায় ছাহাম প্রার্থী বিবাদীদের দরখাস্ত না সজ্ঞুর করা হইল।”

Against the said the order petitioners preferred Civil Revision in which the learned District Judge affirmed the order of the trial court holding similar view. It appears from the record that no appeal was filed in this case against the preliminary decree. 

13. A preliminary decree for partition establishes the right of the plaintiffs to partition. Pursuant to section 97 of the Civil Procedure Code a party is debarred from challenging the correctness of a preliminary decree in an appeal against the final decree. So ordinarily the petitioners cannot go behind the preliminary decree and show that it was wrong. 

14. Section 97 of the Code of Civil Procedure runs as follows : 
97 : Where any party aggrieved by a preliminary decree passed after the _ commencement of this Code does not appeal from such decree, he shall be precluded from disputing its correctness in any appeal which may be preferred from the final decree. 

15. On a plain reading of section 97 it appears that appeal is entertain able against a preliminary decree passed in a partition suit. 

16. In the case of Bittan Devi Vs. Rudra Sen Bajpai, reported in AIR 1966 All 601, their Lordships held : 
"The courts of law cannot go behind the decree and have to take further steps on the basis of the decree already passed. Consequently if the preliminary decree passed in the' partition suit does not contain any declaration as to the rights of the defendants, their application for partition or separation of their share shall not be maintainable till they have the preliminary decree suitably modified but once the preliminary decree contains a declaration as to the defendant's share, they can, even after the passing of the preliminary decree, take steps for the separation of their shares." 

17. In the instant case, since the decree is in preliminary form and final decree is yet to be drawn up, the petitioner can prefer appeal against the preliminary decree. On perusal of the record it is also apparent that the petitioners suffered for no fault of them but in view of the provisions of law and the decision referred above, I am of the opinion that their proper remedy lies in the court of appeal against the preliminary decree which can be filed any time before final, decree is drawn up. 

18. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case and in view of the decision referred here in above, I hold that the learned District Judge did not commit any error of law resulting in an error in such decision occasioning failure of justice in passing the impugned order and there is nothing to interfere with the same. 

19. In the result, the Rule is discharged. 

20. However, there will be no order as to costs. 

21. The order of stay granted at the time of issuance of the Rule is hereby vacated.

 22. Communicate the order at once.

End.

full_judgment:
Mahmudul Amin Chowdhury, J : These two First Appeal Nos. 256 of 1997 and 05 of 1998 are taken up together for judgment as both these two appeals arises out of the same judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 54 of 1995 by the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Narayanganj. The learned Subordinate Judge by his judgment dated 24/.1997 decreed the suit for partition. 

2. The short fact leading to these two appeals are that one Bina Roy Chowdhury instituted the aforesaid suit alleging that the suit land along with other lands originally belonged to Haridash Roy Chowdhury in 8 Anna's share and Jagat Hari Roy Chowdhury and Madhushudhan Roy Chowdhury belonged to 4 Anna's share in each and they were possessing the same in ejmali property. Haridash Roy Chowdhury instituted Title Suit No. 67 of 1961 before the 4th Court of Subordinate Judge, .Dhaka for partition impleading Haridash Roy Chowdhury and Madhushudhan Roy Chowdhury therein. Then on 28.8.1963 the suit was decreed on compromise and by that decree Haridash Roy Chowdhury got the entire suit property of that suit. This Haridash Roy Chowdhury was killed by the Pak Army on 2.4.1971 in Kha schedule land. He left behind the plaintiff as his wife and defendant No. 1 Amullya Roy Chowdhury who is his son and they inherited the property left behind by Haridash Roy Chowdhury. The further case of the plaintiff is that after the death of Haridash Roy Chowdhury the plaintiff went to Sherpur Town and started living there and from there managing Ga and Gha schedule property which she got by amicable partition. She also got Ka and Kha schedule property and possesses the part of the same through Bharatias. It is the further case of the plaintiff that though there was an amicable partition of the property defendant No. 1 as raising claim of Ka and Kha schedule property and he is also planning to transfer Ga schedule property. It is her case that unless the partition by metes and bounds is effected there shall arise complications. During the pendency of the suit an amendment was made wherein it has been alleged that defendant No. 1 for illegal gains transferred Kha schedule property to defendant No. 2 on 22.2.95 by registered kabala, though he was not entitled to transfer that. The plaintiff also prayed for declaration that the said kabala is ille-gal and void. It is also her case that inspite of repeated demands the defendant No. 1 was refusing to effect partition of the suit property for which the plaintiff had to institute the present suit. 

3. Before the trial Court defendants 1 and 2 contested the suit by filing separate written statements, Defendant No. 1 admitted that the suit land was originally belonged to his father Haridash Roy Chowdhury and that the plaintiff is his step mother. But his case is that plaintiff has not acquired any Saleable or partiable interest in the suit property but she got simply her life interest. His further case is that he is possessing the suit property through Bharaties and residing in part of the same. His further case is that he has allowed the plaintiff to enjoy part of Ka schedule property and also getting rent from the tenants. His further case is that he is living in Gha schedule property along with his family. His further case is that he has already transferred Kha schedule property to defendant No. 2 on a proper consideration who was in possession of the same. He has denied the plaintiffs claim that he rejected her demand of partition. 

4. The clear case of defendant No. 2 in his written statement is that he on 22.8.95 purchased Kha schedule properly from defendant No. 1 on a valuable consideration and got possession and he has mutated his name in different registers. His further case is that as his purchased land is not the homestead of the plaintiff the prayer made under Section 4 of the Partition Act cannot be maintained. 

5. Before the trial Court both the sides adduced oral and documentary evidence in support of their respective claims. The learned Subordinate Judge then by the aforesaid judgment decreed the suit in part. On being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree passed in the aforesaid suit the plaintiff and defendant No. 1 preferred these two separate appeals. 

6. Mr. A.B. Roy Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellant in F.A. No. 256 of 1997 led us through the judgment of the trial Court and the evidence on record and he submits that from the perusal of the judgment it would appear that without understanding the implication of partition by metes and bounds the learned Subordinate Judge himself distributed the land amongst the claimants. it has been argued that in a suit for partition the properties are distributed amongst the claimants by metes and bounds which has not been done in the present case. It is also sub-mitted that the trial Court wrongly construed the provision of Section 4 of the Partition Act and came to the incorrect finding that the plaintiffs prayer was made under Section 4 of the Partition Act cannot be maintained. 

7. The learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondent No. 1 on the other hand submits that though there is no dispute on the genealogy given by the plaintiff, but the fact remains that the plaintiff has only life interest in the suit property which cannot be partitioned. It is submitted that the plaintiff can enjoy the property during her life time and thereafter it will devolved to the other co-sharers. It is further submitted that with her permission and knowledge Kha schedule property was transferred to defendant No. 2 and as such a petition filed under Section 4 of the Partition Act cannot be maintained. It has further been argued that as Kha schedule property is not the dwelling house of the plaintiff and defendant No. 1 this cannot be pre-empted under Section 4 of the Partition Act. 

8. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondent No. 2 assailed the order portion of the judgment passed by the learned Subordinate Judge. He submitted that though partition was allowed but it was not allowed by metes and bounds and the trial Court committed wrong in passing the such judgment. He submits that, the property will distributed by metes and bounds which has not been done in the present suit. He further submits that as defendant No. 2 with his good money purchased Kha schedule property from the admitted co-sharer he can maintain the property and this may not be considered in case of partition of the suit property. Agreeing with the submission made by the learned Advocate for the appellant Mr. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed submit-ted that though the evidence was led from both the sides the writing of judgment and determination of the points at issue were not property done by the learned Subordinate Judge. He also agreed with the submission made by the learned Advocate for the respondent No. 1 on the point of applicability of Section 4 of the Partition Act in respect of Kha schedule property which his client purchased. 

9. From the submissions made by the learned Advocates of both the sides and from the perusal of the available materials it appears that there was no dispute on the genealogy as set up by the plaintiff in the plaint. It is not disputed that the suit property was inherited by plaintiff and defendant No. I from Haridash Roy Chowdhury. Plaintiff is the widow of Haridash Roy Chowdhury and defendant No. 1 is her step son. 

10. In this case the learned Advocates of both the sides assailed the judgment on common point and that is the writings of the judgment is such a partition suit was not in accordance with law. The learned Advocates contended that the trial Court while writing the judgment has not followed the principle of distribution of saham by metes and bounds and on that point the judgment cannot be supported. We have gone through the judgment and it appears that the learned Subordinate Judge himself took the trouble on distributing the suit property amongst the three claimants without understanding that a Partition is to be effected by metes and bounds an all the properties in suit are not of the some valuation. On going through the judgment partionlarly the portion wherein he dealt with the distribution of the property it appears that the learned Subordinate Judge has not followed the principle of law in passing a decree in such a suit for partition. There should ought not to have been a preliminary decree to be effected by distribution of saham by metes and bounds and the preliminary decree ought to have culminated as a final decree which found very much absent in the present case. On this ground alone the appeal would have been disposed of. But a very important question has been raised an regards applicability of Section 4 of the Partition Act and for that matter we want to decide the same. 

11. Section 4 of the partition Act provides that where a share of a dwelling-house belonging to an undivided family has been transferred to a person who is not a member of such family, and such transferred sues for partition, the court shall, if any member of the family being a shareholder shall undertake to buy the share of such transferee, make a valuation of such share in such manner as it thinks fit, and direct the sale of such share to such shareholder and may give all necessary and proper directions in that behalf. The applicability of Section 4 are: (1) That the property must be a dwelling house; (2) It must belong to an undivided family ; (3) There must be transfer of a share of the dwelling house; (4) The transferee must be a person who is not a member of the undivided family; (5) There must be a suit for partition (6) One or more members of the undivided family must undertake to purchase the shares of the transferee. The above fundamental requirements of law must be satisfied before the benefit of Section 4 of the Partition Act can be claimed by a member of the undivided family. 

12. Now let as examine whether the plaintiff has succeeded in fulfilling the requirements as mentioned above. Admitted the plaintiff filed the petition under Section 4 of the Partition Act for pre-empting Kha schedules property and admittedly this Kha schedule property has been inherited by the plaintiff and defendant No. 1 and it also an admitted fact that this property was transferred by defendant No. 1 and defendant No. 2 and that this defendant No. 2 is not a member of the undivided family and the present suit is a suit for partition and that the plaintiff undertook to purchase the share of the transferee. Out of the 6 preconditions five conditions are in favour of the plaintiff. Now the question remains as regards the dwelling-house. Now what is the meaning of the words dwelling house. In this case admittedly the plaintiff is not residing or ever resided in Kha schedule property which was purchased by defendant No. 2. There is no evidence that it was a family dwelling-house. But it transpired that those were occupied by some other persons though under the plaintiff and defendant No. 1. It is in evidence that the plaintiff was residing at Sherpur Town after the death of her husband and then she shifted to Narayanganj. So by no stretch of imagination that it cannot be found that the Kha schedule property is the dwelling-house of the plaintiff. So for transacting the Section 4 of the Partition Act the main ingredient is that the property in question of dwelling house has not been proved. The plaintiff failed to lead any evidence to prove that. It may be that the property is meant for human habitation but that cannot be a ground to transact Section 4 of the Partition Act is must be the dwelling-house of the undivided family. The kha schedule property may be a dwelling-house but it was not under direct occupation of the plaintiff and defendant No. 1 and the plaintiff was not residing in that house when the suit for partition was filed: When there is no evidence that the undivided family occupied Kha schedule property in view of the consistent decision of the higher courts of the subcontinent we hold that Section 4 of the Partition Act has no manner of application in the present case. Two decisions on this point has been cited before us. The first one is AIR 1940 (Rangoon) 53 (J.C. Chatterji & others Vs. Maung Myo & another) and 20 DLR 489 (Muhammad Habibullah & another Vs. Moulvi Saleh Chowdhury & others). In both these decisions it has been clearly stated what is the meaning of wards dwelling-house and there is no deviation from these views subsequently. The learned Advocate for the appellant failed to bring out or cite any other decision which has deviated from the aforesaid two decisions. We have considered these two decisions and also the facts and circumstances of the cases and we find nothing to disagree with these two decisions. 

13. Thus, after consideration of the materials on record and the relevant laws we hold that the plaintiff failed to make out any case under Section 4 of the Partition Act. 

14. The learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondent No. 1 submitted that a Hindu Widow is only entitled to life interest on the property loft behind by her husband and that property cannot be partitioned. She will continue to enjoy the property and after her death it will defer to the other heirs. It is further submitted that a Hindu Widow cannot maintain a' suit for partition in respect of agricultural lands. As against this Mr. A. B. Roy Chowdhury the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff appellant submits that under Section 3 of the Hindu Women rise to Property Act A Hindu Widow becomes a complete owner and co-sharer of the property and she has a right to claim of a partition. Her status quo is to be construed is that of is not under a Hindu law and in support of submission he placed reliance in the case of Roy Kishori Saha Vs. Mohammad Motaleb Ali and others, reported in 1982 DCR 55. It has been held in this decision that under Section 3 of the Hindu Women Rights to the Property Act, 1937 it would appear that during her life time a Hindu Widow is a complete owner and co-sharer of any property or holding in question with the right to claim partition. In view of this clear provision of the aforesaid Act and considering the evidence on record we hold that the trial Court has not committed any illegality and wrong in holding that the plaintiff is entitled to partition, even though she has only life interest in the property left behind by her husband. 

15. Now as regards the objection raised that a Hindu Widow cannot seek partition in respect of agricultural lands. We have gone through the Khatians produced before the trial Court and it appears that the lands in question are not agricultural lands these are all non-agricultural lands and when the lands are non-agricultural a partition may be effected at the instance of a Hindu Widow. 

16. Thus, after consideration of the materials on record and after hearing the learned Advocates of both the sides we hold that the learned Subordinate Judge has both committed any wrong or Illegality in ordering partition of the suit property. But he has committed a mistake while distributing the saham which has not been done by metes and bounds. It appears that he has distributed the property leaving aside Kha schedule property which was sold by the defendant No. 1 to defendant No. 2 but that has also must come with the partition and this may be allotted to defendant No. I which admittedly was inherited by the plaintiff and defendant No. 1. It. is well-settled that a co-sharer and specific possession may retain its position and transferred his possessed land to a third party and in case of partition this transferred land will be allotted to the transferor but this must come within the partition. The trial Court it appears that committed wrong in keeping aside this transferred land while passing the order of distribution and that is commit-ted a gross wrong and illegality. 

17. Having given our anxious consideration to materials on record and after hearing the learned Advocates of both the sides we hold that this is a fit case where this Court should interfere and set aside the judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge in the afore-said suit and we are inclined to send the case back to the trial Court for fresh hearing and disposal of the matter from the stage of hearing of the argument by the learned Advocates of both the sides as recording of fresh evidence is found to be not necessary. 

18. Court-fees paid are correct. 

19. The appeals are allowed without any order as to casts. 

20. The judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Narayanganj in Title Suit No. 54 of 1995 is hereby set aside, and the case is sent back to the trial Court on remand for fresh disposal from the Stage of argument in the light of the observations made above. 

21. The learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Narayanganj is hereby directed to disposed of suit within next 4(four) months from the date of receipt of record from this Court with notice to the parties through their respective lawyers. 

22. The office is directed to send down the lower Court records at once.

	End.
