Mr. Md. Abdur Rashid, J: This Rule was obtained by the successors-in-interest of the plaintiff, late Sultan Ahmed against the judgment and decree dated 16-06-94 passed by the Additional District Judge, 4th Court, Chittagong in Other Appeal No. 146 of 1985 reversing those dated 28-01-85 passed by the Upazila Munsif at Upazila Mirsharai, Chittagong in Other Suit No. 11 of 1982; and dismissing the suit.

2. On 21-02-82 the said predecessor-in-interest of the present petitioners as plaintiff instituted the suit for recovery of possession of the suit land purportedly under Section-95 read with Section-95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The suit land is a tank with surrounding banks measuring 0.03 acre of Plot No. 8430 and 0.23 of Plot No. 8431 appertaining to R S Khatian No. 1585 of Mouja Durgapur, PS Mirsharai in the District of Chittagong.

3. By three sale deeds registered on 22-04-74 the plaintiff transferred the suit land to the defendant No. 3 and the same date defendant No. 3 executed and registered a deed of Ekrarnama promising to reconvey the suit land to the plaintiff or his heirs on receipt of Taka 6,000 any time within 30th Chaitra of any year. Pursuant to the transfer, the plaintiff made over possession of the suit land to the defendant No. 3.

4. Thereafter, the plaintiff offered Taka 6,000 first to the defendant No. 3 and then, to the defendants Nos. 1 and 2 and requested them for return of the suit land. But none of the defendants paid any heed to his request. Hence, he was p constrained to institute the suit.

5. The suit was contested by the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 by filing a joint written statement, Their main case is that the deed of Ekrarnama was neither executed nor presented nor registered by the defendant No. 3. They had no knowledge of existence of the said deed of Ekrarnama. Rather, they purchased the suit land by registered sale deeds dated 05-07-75 and 28-02-79 from the defendant No. 3 with the knowledge and consent of the plaintiff The plaintiff attested their sale deeds. Their further case is that the transaction between the plaintiff and defendant No. 3 is an out and out sale. There is no question of any mortgage ever entered into by the plaintiff and defendant No. 3. The defendants No, 1 and 2 further claimed to be bona fide purchasers for value without notice of the Ekrarnama. They asserted that the plaintiff was estopped from raising any question as to any sort of mortgage and thereby not entitled to any decree.

6. The trial court decreed the suit with out costs and directed the defendants to deliver the possession of the suit land ii favour of the plaintiff within 30 days. Or appeal at the instance of the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 the appellate court allowed the, appeal and set aside the judgment and decree of the trial court and dismissed the suit.

7. Being aggrieved by the decree of the appellate court, the present petitioner: moved this court in revision under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure an obtained the Rule as stated above.

8. Mr. S. N. Goswami, learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners submitted that the court of appeal below did not consider the entire evidence on record. The finding of the appellate court that th4 'Ekrarnama' exhibit 1 is forged and created for the purpose of the suit is not based or due consideration of the evidence or record. Secondly, he submitted that the finding of the appellate court that the defendant: Nos. I and 2 are purchasers for value with out notice of the Ekrarnama is also no based on any evidence and as such, is equally not valid and binding.

<u>9. On the other hand, Mr. Abu Salek learned senior Advocate appearing for opposite parties Nos. 1 and 2, submitted the suit for possession was dismissed b:s. the appellate court below on due consider action of the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence, both oral and documentary on record. The findings of the appellate court that the Ekrarnama forged and created and that the defendant 1 and 2 are purchasers for value without notice of the Ekrarnama are finding on facts and were concluded by the findings of the final court of facts. Such findings do not call for any interference by this court under Section-115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In support of his submission, he also cited, on the scope of revision under Section-115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the following cases,</u>

<u>a. Shamser Ali v. Most Kafizan Bibi, reported in 44 DLR (AD) 234,</u>

<u>b. Rupe Jahan Begum v. Lutfe Ali, reported in 49 DLR (AD) 73 and</u>

<u>c. Jahanara Begum v. Md. Aminul Islam, reported in 50 DLR (AD) 52. He also referred to the case of Tazal Islam v. Md. Affan, reported in 17 DLR 613 on bona fide purchaser for value without notice.</u>

10. In view of such submissions, I feel, it is my duty to examine closely the entire evidence, both oral and documentary on record in the facts and circumstances of the case in order to find whether the decision arrived at by the court of appeal calls for any interference by this court.

11. The plaintiff examined 2 witnesses including himself while the defendants 1 and 2 examined 4 witnesses including themselves. Besides, the Ekrarnama, i.e. the deed of reconveyance which was adduced and marked as exhibit 1. the sale deeds executed by the plaintiff in favour of the defendant 3 marked as exhibit 2, 2 (A) and 2 (B) and the sale deeds of the defendants 1 and 2 from defendant 3 marked as exhibit A (2) and A (3).

12. The case of the plaintiff was that by 3 registered sale deeds exhibits 2, 2 (A) and 2 (B), he transferred the suit land to defendant 3 on 22.04,74 and the defendant 3 in his turn, by another deed of conveyance registered, exhibit 1 on the same date agreed to reconvey the said land to the plaintiff on receipt of Taka 6,000. Defendant 3 or defendants 1 and 2 did not reconvey the suit land even on demands. So, the plaintiff was constrained to institute the suit on 21.02.82 for recovery of the suit land. as he was entitled to restoration of the land under Section-95 read with Section-95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 for the sale by the deeds exhibits 2 to 2 (B) with the agreement to reconvey, Ekrarnama, exhibit 1 must be construed to be a complete usufructuary mortgage not exceeding seven years.

13. Opposing such claim of the plaintiff, defendants -1 and .2 averred that they purchased the suit land with the knowledge and consent of the plaintiff by their deeds exhibits A (2) and A (3) registered on 05.07.75 and 28.02.79 respectively. Defendant No. 1 purchased 0.12 acre of Plot No. 8431 while defendant No. 2 purchased rest 0.03 acre of Plot No. 8430 and 0.11 acre of 8431. They further asserted that plaintiff attested their deeds of sale. They had no notice of the agreement for reconveyance. They were protected as bona fide purchasers for value without notice.

14. They also challenged the genuineness of the Ekrarnama. They asserted that the defendant 3 did not give the deed. Defendant 3 did neither execute the deed nor any affidavit in support of the deed for registration. It was created by the plaintiff.

15. The trial court held that the deeds of sale and the agreement for reconveyance together constitutes an usufructuary mortgage not exceeding seven years under Sections-95 and 95A of the State Acquisition Tenancy Act. and that the defendants 1 and 2 was aware of the Ekrarnama as they admitted that they knew the original title deeds of defendant 3 i.e. exhibits 2, 2A and 2B were in the custody of the plaintiff .

16. The appellate court below, on the other hand, found that the plaintiff failed to prove the genuineness of exhibit 1, Ekrarnama. Then, he held  that the Ekrarnama between the plaintiff and defendant 3 is forged and created by them with an eye to grab the suit land. Reasons for such findings, as the appellate court. mentioned, are that the plaintiff is the father-in-law of defendant 3, the plaintiff attested the sale deeds of defendants 1 and 2, exhibits A(2) and A(3), that the plaintiff did not deny his signature on exhibit A(3), that the plaintiff failed to examine the

scribe and all the attesting witnesses of exhibit I. Ekrarnama.

17. The appellate court further held that defendants 1 and 2 are purchasers for value without notice of the Ekraniama, exhibit I. probably, on the reasons stated above. a also noted that the plaintiff could not produce any competent and reliable evidences to prove that the defendants had knowledge of the Ekrarnama.

18. I find from the record that the sale deeds, exhibits 2 and 2A were executed on 20.04.74, and exhibit 28 was executed on 01.04.74 by the plaintiff in favour of defendant No, 3. All the three deeds were registered on 24.04.74. The Ekrarnama, exhibit was also executed and registered by the defendant 3 on .24.04.74. I also find the affidavit was sworn and signed by the defendant 3 in support of the Ekrarnama. In the Ekrarnama, it is written.

‘আপনার সহিত আমার কথা রহিল যে আপনি বা আপনার ওয়ারিশান আমি বা আমার ওয়ারিশানরক যে কোন ৩০শে চৈত্র মাসের মধ্যে বর্ণিত কবলা ক্রয়ের পণের সমুদয় টাকা আদায় করিয়া দিলে টাকা গ্রহণে ছাড়িয়া দিতে বাধ্য হিলাম বা থাকিবে। যদি আপোষে টাকা গ্রহণ না করি তবে আপনি বা আপনার ওয়ারিশান আদালতে টাকা জমা দিয়া জমিজমা দখল পাইতে সক্ষম থাকিবেন।’

19. The Ekrarnama was written by M Amir Max and witnessed by Abu Backkar Siddique and Ahmedur Rahman. In adducing the Ekrarnama. the plaintiff testified that defendant 3 gave him the Ekrarnama. Amir Bux had written the Ekrarnama. During cross-examination, he stated that the Ekrarnama was executed and registered the same date, In the Mirsharai Sub-Registrar's office. Defendant 3 had also sworn an affidavit in support of the Ekrarnama.

20. Abu Backkar Siddique, an attesting witness to the Ekrarnama was examined as P.W. 2. He testified that he was a licensed deed writer. Exhibit 1 was Written and read before him. Defendant 3 executed the same. He was a witness to the deed. In cross-examination, he further said that on 22.04.74 the deed was executed. Amir Bux wrote that. He denied the suggestion that it was not true that defendant 3 put his signature before him. He also denied that the deed was fabricated.

21. it is true that the other attesting witness M Ahmedur Rahman and the scribe were not examined. Now, the question is whether the deed, exhibit I can be held to be not proved according to law for non-examination of the scribe and the other attesting witness.

<u>22. The exhibit I, Ekrarnama is a registered deed. So, there arises under Sections-59 and 60 of the Registration Act read with Sections-79 and 114 (illustration e) of the Evidence Act a presumption that it was duly presented and registered by defendant 3. Such presumption is, however, rebuttable. But no evidence in rebuttal of such presumption was adduced by the defendants 1 and 2. Even, they did not take any step to examine defendant 3 who could have come to the court and denied to have executed the Ekrarnama. The Ekrarnama would then have a decent burial. A licensed deed writer PW-2 on oath testified that the deed was written before him by the scribe, Amir Bux and executed by the defendant 3 The plaintiff also deposed in the same line on the writing of the deed and its execution. Sections-67 and 68 of the Evidence Act provide for proof of signature, handwriting and execution of a deed. Ekrarnama is not required to be attested under the law. Even, then it was attested by two witnesses. Any attesting witness can prove the writing and execution of the deed. The appellate court did neither discard nor disbelieve the evidence of PW-2, Abu Backkar Siddique. also do not find any reason to disbelieve the evidence on the writing and execution of the Ekrarnama. In view of the law and the evidence as stated above, why the execution of Ekrarnama, exhibit I should not be held to have been proved is not understood. So, without discarding and or disbelieving the evidence of Pik- 1 and 2 and considering the relevant laws, the appellate court erred in law to hold that the plaintiff filed to prove the Ekrarnama.</u>

23. I have also gone through the writ-ten statement as well the evidence of the defendants 1 and 2. They did not make out any case that the plaintiff and defendant 3 as father-in-law and son-in-law created the Ekrarnama to grab the suit land as held by the appellate court. So, I could not find any basis for the appellate court in rushing to the conclusion that "the Ekrarnama in between the plaintiff and defendant 3 as father-in-law and son-in-law is a forged and created by them to grab the suit land. This Is nobody's case, at least not the case of the defendants 1 and 2. Moreover, it cannot be accepted that one year or five years after the defendants 1 and 2 would. purchase the  land, so the plaintiff created or fabricated the document on 22.04.74.

<u>24. Now, let me see how far the finding of the appellate court that the defendants 1 and 2 are purchasers for value without notice of the Ekrarnama is based on evidence be record and the law. Are their transactions really protected either under Section-41 of the Transfer of Property Act or under Section-115 of the Evidence Act? If one wants to be protected under Section-41 of the Transfer of Property Act, he is required to prove that he took all reasonable care to ascertain the title of his vendor. He inquired at least in the local Sub-Registrar's office to know if the land had any charge or encumbrance or not to establish his bona fide. He would naturally try to get all the documents of title and possession from his vendor. Onus is very heavy on him. There is no onus on the other side, as was wrongly placed by the appellate court. The law is now settled. Section-41 T P Act is an exception to ordinary rule that the transferor cannot convey a greater title to the transferee than he himself has and has to be construed strictly. If any one seeks. protection purportedly either under Section-41 of the Transfer of property Act or tinder of the Evidence Act, he must prove the facts entitling him the benefits under either of the laws. He is required to prove that 'he, after taking reasonable care to ascertain that the transfer or had power to make the transfer, acted in good faith.' I am supported by the authorities in case of Sunder lcuer v Udey Ram, reported in AIR 1944 Allahabad 42 (page 54 c. d) and Ambabai v. H R Dant reported in AIR 1948 Nagpur 367 (pares 50 and 51). The defendants 1 and 2 pleaded that they were bona fide purchasers for value without notice of the Ekrarnama. But they did neither plead nor lead any evidence that they took any steps to ascertain the title of their vendor, defendant 3 or their purchased land, i.e. the suit land did not have any charge or encumbrance. They did not make any inquiry even in the local registration office. They did not want to get the documents of title or possession. In their deeds, exhibit A(2) and A(3) though executed and registered about four years apart, it is written in verbatim, to trace the title, the defendant 3 is খরিদ সূত্রে মালিক দখলকার ও মালিক বটে’ This vital fact of purchase from the plaintiff was deliberately suppressed exhibits A(2) and A(3). Purpose was very clear, not to divulge the knowledge about the Ekrarnama. In his deposition, defendant 1 as DW-1 stated that the plaintiff transferred the land to the defendant 3 by an out and out sale. In cross-examination, he admitted that defendant 3 on being asked told him that the original Kabala was lying with the plaintiff. He did not try to obtain the Kabala. Defendant 2 as DW-2 deposed in the same vein that original Kabala was with the plaintiff and he did not try to get the Kabala. Both of them, however, stated that they purchased seeing the copy of the Kabla. But they did not adduce the copy to probe their bona fide it is, therefore, cult to accept such an explanation.</u>

<u>25. Their main case is that the plaintiff attested their Kabalas. So, they asserted that they purchased with the knowledge and/or consent of the plaintiff. It is true the plaintiff attested the Kabala of defendant 1 dated 05.07.75, exhibit A(2) only. But he did not attest the Kabala of defendant 2 dated 28.02.79, exhibit A(3) as was wrongly found by the appellate court. The plaintiff explained in his deposition that he put his signature on the request of the defendant and that he thought that the deed was in respect of other land. He also stated that they live as neighbours. The law on attestation is also clean As it was ruled by the Privy Council long back in 1928 in the case of Bhagwan v. Ujagar, reported in AIR PC 20 that, attestation of a deed by itself estops a man from denying nothing whatever except that he witnessed the execution of the deed, and by itself it does not show that he consented to the transaction which the documents effects. In the case of Sunder Kuer v. Udey Ram, reported in AIR 1944 Allahabad 42, it was further stated that,</u>

<u>'It does not by itself convey any knowledge of the contents of the document, and reliance cannot be placed on it alone for the purpose of establishing that the person attesting the document consented to the transaction which it effects, and knowledge of the contents ought not to be inferred from the mere fact of attestation. At the same time, it is well settled that an attestation may take place in circumstances which would show that the person attesting the document did in fact know all its contents.'</u>

<u>The law was again stated in the case of Nainsukhdas v. Gowardhandas, reported in AIR 1968 Nagpur 110.</u>

<u>The defendants' 1 and 2 did not only take any reasonable care either to ascertain the title of their vendor, defendant 3 or to find if the land had any charge or encumbrance but also suppressed in their deeds from whom their vendor, defendant 3 got the land. In view above evidences, the defendants 1 and 2 cannot be held to be bona fide purchasers without notice and as such, protected under Section-41 of the Transfer of Property Act.</u>

<u>And in the circumstances, by attestation to deed exhibit A(2), the plaintiff cannot be held to have knowledge of the contents of the deed, exhibit A(2) in order to be estopped under Section-115 of the Evidence Act for claiming restoration of the suit land under Sections-95. and 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950.</u>

26. For the reasons stated above, the findings of the appellate court that the Ekrarnama is forged and created and that the defendants 1 and 2 are purchasers without notice of the Ekrarnama must be held to have been arrived at by misreading or non-reading of the evidence on record and on total ignorance of the relevant principles of law as stated above. Such findings, however, on facts cannot be sustained in law. Upon such erroneous findings, the appellate court allowed the appeal and dismissed the suit. Such decision of the appellate court has definitely resulted in such an error that his occasioned failure of justice. To correct such an error, discretion under Section-115 of the Code of Civil Procedure has been given to this Division. In exercise of the discretion under Section-115 of the Code of Civil Procedure such error must be corrected by this Division.

27. I have examined the single bench decision in the case of Tazal Hoque v. Md. Allan reported in 17 DLR 613 as cited by Mr. Salek. After the decision, I find, the law on usufructuary mortgage has undergone a change on insertion of Section-95A in the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act by the President Order No. 88 of the 1972. During the appeal, the plaintiff, Sultan Ahmed died on 18.05.91. The present petitioners were substituted in his place. Now, the petitioners who have also the covenant under the Ekrarnama as quoted above to get reconveyance have become entitled to restoration of possession of the entire suit land as prayed for. Moreover, the defendants 1 and 2 have not been found to be bona fide purchasers without notice of the Ekrarnama. Facts of the case are also quite distinguishable from the facts of the present case. So, the trial court rightly held that the sale deeds exhibits 2 series along with the deed of agreement, Ekrarnama, exhibit 1 do in fact constitute an usufructuary mortgage not exceeding seven years and that the defendants 1 and 2 were aware of the Ekrarnama. The decision of the trial court that the plaintiff is entitled to get restoration of possession of the suit land from the defendants 1 and 2 under Section-95 read with Section-95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is accordingly affirmed.

28. In the result, the rule is made absolute. No order as to cost. The judgment and decree of the appellate court are set aside and the decree of the trial court is restored. The suit is decreed. The defendants 1 and 2 are directed as was directed by the trial court to restore possession of the suit land to the petitioners within two months from the receipt of the record by the trial court. Let the record be sent down at once.

29. Consequently, the order of this court directing the parties to maintain status quo granted earlier is hereby vacated.

End.

Md. Hamidul Haque J : By this Rule the opposite parties have been called upon to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 27.5.89 passed by the learned District Judge. Noakhali, in Title Appeal No. 104 of 1988 should not be set aside, or such other or further order or orders as to this court may seem fit and proper. 

2. The facts, which are relevant for the purpose of disposal of this Rule are stated below :-The opposite party No. 1 filed Title suit No. 260 of 1979 in the court of subordinate Judge. Noakhali for a decree for Specific Performance of Contract. His case is that the defendant No. I Md. Saidul Huq was the owner of the suit land measuring 971/2decimal land. The defendant No. I offered to sell the suit land to the plaintiff and the plaintiff agreed to purchase the same for Tk. 20.437/- and Tk. 20.000/- was paid in advance on 8.4.76 and a bainapatra was executed on that date and possession of the property was also delivered. It was settled that the defendant No. 1 after receiving the balance amount on consideration within Magh. 1385 B.S. would execute and register a sale deed in favour of the plaintiff in respect of the suit land. The plaintiff offered the balance amount but the defendant did not accept the amount. The last offer was made by the plaintiff on 13th Magh, 1385 B..S. but the defendant refused to accept the balance amount and to execute register a sale deed in favour to the plaintiff. By amending the plaint the plaintiff further stated that with a fraudulent intention, the defendant No. 1 instead of executing and registering the sale deed in favour of the plaintiff,_ collusively created 2 kabalas dated 16.7.78 transferring the entire suit land in favour of the defendant Nos. 3-6. These defendant are minor daughter of Abdul Monim Chowdhury through whose negotiation the plaintiff entered into an agreement with the defendant No. 1 to purchase the suit land. Abdul Monim Chowdhury being fully aware of the agreement of the plaintiff, with a malafide intention created the kabalas in collusion with the defendant No. 1 without any consideration. 

3. The defendant Nos. 3-6 contested the suit by filing written statement claiming that the bainapatra of the plaintiff is forged and antidated. The case is that the defendant No. 1 offered, to sell the property at Tk. 30,000/- and the talk of sale was held with the father of these defendants who agreed to purchase the suit land and thereafter on receiving the entire consideration money, the defendant No. 1 executed a sale deed and also delivered possession to the Father of defendant. The elder brother of the father of these defendants named Abdul Hye used to look after the property after the purchase. The defendants claim that the plaintiff did not get any possession of the basis his alleged bainapatra but the sons of the plaintiff tried to disturb possession of the defendants and as such these defendants filed Title suit No. 317 of 1979 in the 3rd court of Munsif, Noakhali for a decree for permanent injunction and as the defendants of that 
suit could not show their right, title, interest and possession in the suit land as order of temporal)/ injunction was issued against them. 

4.The learned subordinate judge, on consideration of the evidence adduced by the parties at the time of trial, come to the finding that the bainapatra was antidated and that the plaintiff did not get possession of the suit land on the basis of his alleged banapatra. The learned subordinate judge also found that the purchase of the defendants was genuine and the they had been in possession sices their purchase. On these findings, the learned subordinate judge dismissed the suit. The plaintiff then filed Title Appeal No. 104 of 1988 in the court of the learned District judge. Noakhali which was heard and disposed of by the learned District judge himself by impuged judgment dated 27.5.89. The learned District judge reversed the judgment and decree of the learned lower court after coming to a decision that the bainapatra was genuine and not antidated and that the contesting of contesting defendants had knowledge of the Glarier contract between the plaintiff and defendant No. I So. the learned District judge allowed the appeal and decreed the suit. 

5. The contesting defendant Nos. 3-6, by filing this revisional application, challenged the validity of the decision of the learned appellate Court The main ground them in this revisional 
application is that the learned appellate court committed an error of law in holding that the father and uncle of the contesting defendants were present at the time of sale and defendants and full 
knowledge of the agreement between the defendant No. 1 and the plaintiff. In fact, the agreements addressed to the court by both the parties centered round the question whether the contesting defendants were percent for vainalede to consideration without notice Of the carrier contract and whether the appellate court committed any error of law in deciding the question. 

6. Mr. A. Baset Majumder, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner at the very out set submits that when the learned appellate court held that the contesting defendant Nos. 3-6 did not claim that they were outside purchaser of vahana consideration without notice of the pro-existing contact the court committed an error if law in deciding the same question. Next, he says that the learned appellate court came to a finding that the father and uncle of these defendants were present in the talk of sale between the plaintiff and defendant No. 1 purely on conjecture and surmise. In this connection he also says that the P.Ws. could not prove that Abdul Monim Chowdhury and Abul Kalam, father and uncle of the contesting defendants were present in the talfof sale. As against these submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioners. Mr. Nikhilesh Dutta, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff opposite party. No. 1 has submitted that the learned appellate court on consideration of the evidence of both the parties held that the father and uncle of the contesting defendants had knowledge of the agreement between the plaintiff and defendant No. 1 however, he has submitted that as the defendant the selves did not claim that they were bonafide purchasers for valuable consideration without notice of the pre-existing agreement, the decision on the point was not so much important. 

7. The original suit was filed for a decree for specific performance of Contract. The plaintiff opposite party No. 1 claims that. the defendant No. the original owner of the suit, land, agreed to sell the suit land to him for a consideration of Tk.20,437/- and on receipt on amount of Tk.20.000/- executed a bainapatra in his favour on 8.4.76 and also delivered possession of the suit land to him. The contesting defendant’s main case is that the bainapatra of the plaintiff is forged and antidated. They claim that after sale of the suit land to them by two kabalas dated 16.7.78, the plaintiff in collusion with the defendant No. 1 created an antidated bainapatra in respect of the suit land. So, the main question as it appears to me, is whether the bainaprtra in genuine or not and whether it is an antideated or not. The learned lower court on consideration of the evidence or record found that the bainaptra was not genuine and it was antidated where as the learned appellate court found that the bainaparta was genuine and it was not antidated rather it was executed on the date as shown in the bainapatra itself. 

8. 1 have found that the two courts arrived at contradictory decisions as regards the bainapatra. On perusal of the judgment of the learned lower court it appears that the court held the bainapatra to be an antidated document merely on the ground that it was written on two sheets of paper using two different pen and ink. The court also held that the 2nd sheet used was an old cartridge paper and such the writing choked. On the other hand, the learned appellate court with reference of the statements of the P.Ws. and also on considering the bainapatra itself found that it was genuine and not at all antidated. 

9. As the two courts arrived at a contradictory decision regarding the bainapatra, 1 myself perused the same and also the statements made by the P.Ws. The bainapatra has been Marked Exhibit. 1. The stamp paper of Tk. 1.50 was purchased by the plaintiff. A. Jabbar from stamp vender named phani Bhushon Sarker on 7.1.76. It further appears that besides the stamp paper, another cartridge paper is also used. The learned lower court held that the two papers, of the binapatra were written with two different pen using different ink but on perusal of the bainapatra 1 find that only the schedule portion at page No. 2 was written by a different pen using different ink but the names of the parties, consideration amount and all other material particulars are written by the same Pen using the same ink. Use of different pen and ink can not be a reason to believe that the document is antidated. All material particulars were written on the stamp paper at page No. 1. 1 find that there is no scope of making it antidated when the first page and half portion of the second page including the date was written by the same pen using same ink. The document can not be considered as antidated only because the schedule was written by a different pen using different ink. 

10. As regards the oral evidence on the point, the plaintiff examined some  of the attesting witnesses named Aminullah (P.W.2) Abu Taher (P.W. 3) and Ali Ahmed (.P.W.5) The plaintiff himself deposed as P.W.1. He says that the bainapatra was written by Mobarak Ali who is not alive. He also says that the two other attesting witnesses Moksed Ali and Ambar Ali are also Read. Next he says that he purchased the stamp paper from Maijdee before one day prior to the date of the bainapatra. He also says that the bainapatra was written two stamp papers. Next he says that Aminullah, Abu Taher, Moksedur Rahman, Joynal were present at the time of bainapatra. I have already found from the stamp paper itself that the same was purchased on 7.4.76 and that the bainapatra was executed on 8.4.76. However, the statement of PM.' 1 that the bainapatra was written two stamp papers though appears to be inconsistent is not unnatural. It is quite natural that could not differentiate between stamp paper and cartridge paper. So the inconsistency is not material at all. P.W.2 Aminullah says that the defendant No. 1 after receiving the advance, executed banapatra. He proved the signature of defendant No. 1 and also said that the stamp paper for writing the bainapatra was supplied by the plaintiff. P.W.3 also says that the defendant. No. 1 after going through the bainapatra and after receiving Tk. 20,000/- executed the bainapatra. He also says that Amanullah, Moksed, Amber Ali, the plaintiff the defendant and the scribe were present at the lime. This witness stated that bainapatra was written using a single pen and same ink. This statement appears to be inconsistent with we have seen in the bainapatra itself. But this also appears to be not at all a material inconsistency. Normally while writing any paper of document, it is written by single pen but replacement of a pen may be necessary when there is no ink in the pan with which writing was started. The inconsistencies noticed by the learned lower court are not at all sufficient hold that the bainapatra was antidated. So, I do not find any reason to hold that the learned appellate court committed any error law in holding that the bainapatra was genuine and not antidated. 

11. Now, the question arises as to whether the defendants can be considered as bonafide purchaser for valuable consideration without notice of the pre-existing agreement between' the plaintiff and defendant No. 1 At the very out set, it struck my mind that the defendants in this suit being the subsequent purchasers have not come with a plea that at the time of their purchased they were not aware of the pre-existing contract between the plaintiff and defendant No. 1. They did not justify their purchase by clamming that their purchase was protected under the provisions of section 27(b) of the specific Relief Act. Now, the question is when the subsequent purchasers themselves did not raise the plea of being bonafide purchaser for valuable consideration without notice of the earlier agreement, the discussion on this question is at all necessary or not. Mr. Basel Majumder, the learned Advocate for the petitioner by referring to case of Mukter Hossain. Khan Vs, Suresh Chandra Dey and others as reported An 42 D.L.R. p. 86. has submitted that the subsequent purchaser has a onus to prove that he purchased the property for valuable consideration on good faith without knowledge of the earlier contract. According to him, the onus of the defendant is shifted to the plaintiff, is if the defendant denies the knowledge of the contract. In this connection, he further submits that the plaintiff could not prove that father of the defendant Abdul Momin Chowdhury negotiated the sale between the plaintiff and the defendant No. 1 or that Abdul Momin Chowdhury and his brother Abdul Kalam were present in the talk of sale. According to him the learned appellate court believed that Abdul Momin Chowdhury was present in the talk of sale only considering the fact that he did not appear as a witness. 

12. On perusal of the judgment of the learned appellate court it appears that the court discussed the circumstances and also the evidence and found that defendant No. 1 in collusion with Abdul Monim Chowdhury created the two kabalas in favour of the defendant Nos. 3-6. The learned court placed to much impotence on the fact that Abdul Momin Chowdhury did not appear in the court to depose as a witness. 1 think that only on this ground it can not be said that Abdul Momin Chowdhury negotiated the sale or was present in the talk of sale. In view of the fact that the defendants did not claim themselves to be bonafide purchasers for valuable consideration without notice of the earlier agreement and also in view of fact that the defendants claim that bainapatra of the plaintiff is antidated, there is no necessity to decide the question whether the defendants are purchaser for valuable consideration without notice of the earlier agreement. 

13. Even if the question as to whether is defendant had knowledge of the earlier contract need not be discussed, the question as to what will be the legal consequence of the purchases of the defendant requires decision. The plaintiff claims that he entered into possession of the suit land on the date of bainapatra and continued to possess the same. The bainapatara is dated 8.4.76. The kabalas of the defendants are of the year 1978. So the question as to whether the plaintiff got possession on the basis of bainapatra is very relevant and important to decide the above question. If the plaintiff was in possession on the basis of bainapatra, the subsequent purchases of the defendants can not be considered as bonafide purchases. So, it is to be decided first whether plaintiff is in possession or the defendant are in possession of the suit land. The learned trial court found that the plaintiff failed to prove his possession and the defendants proves their possession since their purchase. On the other hand, the learned appellate court found that the plaintiff had been in possession , since the bainapatra. 

14. As the two courts have arrived that contradictory decision on the question of possession, it will be convenient to discuss the evidence on this point. The case of the plaintiff is that he got delivery of possession of the suit land immediately after the execution of bainapatra. As P.W. 2 he said that possession was hand over to him at 11. A.M. on 25th Chaitra 1382 B.S. and the witnesses were present at that time. The witnesses stated that writing bainapatra several at about 11, A. M. and was concluded at about 12/12-30. This is vary minor in consistency. P.W. 2, 3 and 5 who are attesting witnesses also said that possession was handed over to plaintiff immediately after execution of the bainapatra and they were present at that time. The learned trial court disbelieved the possession of the plaintiff mainly relying on the following statement of P.W.11. "নালিশী জমির ভিতরে পুকুর আছে। এবং সেখানে আজ মাছ ধরিয়াছে। তবে আঃ মমিন ধরিয়াছে কিনা জানি না।" Only on the basis of the above statement, the learned lower court found that plaintiff was not in possession of the suit land. It appears that the suit land comprises of 971/2 decimal of land appertaining to two plots in one plot 92 decimals and in another plot 51/2  decimals. As regards the existouse of pond in the suit land, the other witnesses except D.W4 did not saw anything. The D.W.4. claims himself to be a Bargadhar under Abdul Momin Chowdhury, father of the contesting defendants. He say that he cultivates eastern half of the suit land under Abdul Momin and there is a pond contiguous to the land which he cultivates. He further says that Momin Miah rear fish in that pond. So, from the statement of P.W. 1 and 4 it appears that there is a pond contiguous to the suit land. Even if Abdul Momin Chowdhury caught fish in that pond, only for that reason in can not be said that the plaintiff is not in possession of the suit land. I have already mentioned that the plaintiff got delivery of possession from the defendant No. 1 and the witness were present at that time Except one witness, the other witnesses described the suit land even by giving dag number and area, On the other hand, the defendant also claim possession. D.W.1. Says that the defendants possess through bargader Sharafat Ali and Reazul Haque, Sharafat Ullah says that he possess half he half of the suit land as bargader and the remaining half is possessed by Rezul Haque under Abdul Momin Chowdhury. In his examination in-chief he could not say weather the plaintiff possess the suit land or not. He has further said in 
his examination in cross that he culltivates western half of the suit land but he could not say dag number and khatian number. He further says that there is dispute in respect of eastern half of the suit-land. He also says that Abdul jabbar harvested paddy of the eastern half D.W.4 is another bargadar, he also could not say dag number of the suit land. He says that he cultivates eastern half of the suit land as bargader the other bargadar sharafat said that Abdul Jabbar hervested crops from the eastern half. The learned lower court did not discuss the entire evidence on the point of possession but on the basis of single statement held that the plaintiff was not in possession. The learned appellate court after discussing the evidence found the decision given by the trial court on the basis of a single statement was not proper. The appellate court also found that the plaintiff contracted to purchases only 5 decimal out of 88 decimals of plot No. 3952 which is pond. It is obvious that there are other co-sharers of that pond. D.W4 says that Abdul Momin Chowdhury had a share in that pond. Naturally, Abdul Momin Chowdhury caught fish on that particular dated. So, it is clear that the learned lower court arrived at a decision on the question of possession without discussing the entire evidence on record. On the other hand, on consideration of the evidence on record, it appears to me that the learned appellate court was not wrong when decided that the plaintiff proved his possession in the suit land. 

15. As regards possession, Mr. Basel Majumder, the learned Advocate of the petitioner has submitted that the defendants filed a suit for permanent injunction against sons of the plaintiff claiming title and possession in the suit land on the basis of their purchase by kabala dated 6.7.78 and when the defendants of that suit failed to prove their prima facie possession in the suit land, the court issued temporary injunction against the sons of the plaintiff, So, according to him the plaintiff can not be in possession of the suit land. I find no reference of this suit in the judgment of the learned lower court, D.Ws. also did not. say anything about this temporary injunction. The plaintiff entered in to possession of the suit land on the basis of the Bainapatra long before the issuance of the temporary injunction. The defendants purchased on 6.7.78 when the plaintiff was in possession. If the plaintiff was in possession of the suit land at the time of the purchase of the defendants it can not be said that the defendants purchased the suit land without making any inquiry as to under what authority the plaintiff had been possessing the same land. The contesting defendants are all minors, the purchases were made in their names by their father Abdul Momin Chowdhury who was circle officer. So, it can be easily said that he was aware of the implication of the possession of the plaintiff when he obtained the kabala in the name of his minor daughters. As the plaintiff was in possession of the suit land. It can not be said that the purchase was Bonafide because the possession of the plaintiff tantamount to notice of his right in the property. Considering this aspect, the purchase made by their father in their names can not considered as bonafide purchase. 

16. Thus considering the legal position and the evidence on recorded. 1 am of the opinion that learned appellate court did not commit any error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. I find no reason to interfere with its decision. In the result, the Rule be discharged with out any order as to costs. 

End.

Mr. A. K. Badrul Huq, J: Delay: Delay : Delay : Laches and Negligence : Laches 
and Negligence : Laches and Negligence have become the theme of all the proceedings under taken by the defendants-petitioner to challenge ex parte decree awarded in favour of plaintiff-opposite parties. 

2. Feeling aggrieved by a judgment and order dated 10.10.1999 recorded by District judge, Cox's Bazar in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 53 , of 1988 affirming judgment and order dated 10.11.1988 passed by learned Assistant Judge, Moheshkhali, Cox's Bazar in Miscellaneous Case No. 18 of 1985 rejecting an application under Order-9, Rule-13 read with Section-151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the defendants-petitioners invoked this Court's Civil Revisional 
Jurisdiction on laying a petition under Section-115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

3. The decision proposed to be given in this Civil Revision petition calls for precise 
recounting of facts only to depict a picture how the defendants petitioners, thanks to the permissiveness of the judicial system, took one after another proceeding for long twenty years over looking that every access to justice should not be misused. The portrayal of essential facts are succinctly stated hereunder: 
(a) The predecessor of Opposite parties Sahera Khatun as plaintiff laid a suit being Other Suit No. 263 of 1969 in the Court of Munsif (New Assistant Judge) Cox's Bazar impleading the predecessor of the present petitioners and others on defendants for a partition of the property describe in schedule to the plaint. The said suit was, subsequently, transferred to the Court of Munsif (Now Assistant Judge), Moheshkhali and renumbered there as Other Suit No. 192 of 
1984. During the pendency of the suit the plaintiff Sahera Khatun died and his heirs, the present opposite parties were substituted as plaintiffs. 
(b) The predecessor of defendants-petitioners appeared in the suit and presented a written statement traversing all the materials allegations made in the plaint. The contesting defendant died during pendency of the suit and his heirs were substituted in his place and they are petitioners in this Civil Revision Petition.
(c) The suit was fixed for preemptory hearing on 20-2-74. The defendants having defaulted in making appearance in the suit, the same was decreed ex parte. Thereafter, a Miscellaneous Case being numbered 193 of 1974 under Order-9, Rule-13 of the Code of Civil Procedure was filed by the defendant-petitioners for 'restoration of the suit to its file and number on setting aside the ex parte decree. The said Miscellaneous Case was allowed ex parte, ex parte decree was set aside and the suit was restored to its file and number. Again, the suit was fixed for preemptory hearing on 1-6-1978. On that date also the defendants-petitioners defaulted in appearing in the suit when the same was called on for hearing. Consequently, the suit was once again decreed ex parte. The defendant-petitioners, thereafter, laid another case being Miscellaneous Case No. 199 of 1980 under Order-9 Rule-13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for restoration of the suit to its file and number on setting aside ex parte decree. The said Miscellaneous Case stood dismissed on contest by the judgment and order dated 16-5-81 by the learned Munsif (Now Assistant Judge) Cox's Bazar. The said judgment and order was set aside by the learned Subordinate Judge, First Court, Cox's Bazar by the judgment and order dated 16-5-81 on allowing an appeal being Miscellaneous Appeal No. 359 of 1981 presented by the defendants-petitioner against the above judgment and order recorded in Miscellaneous Case No. 199 of 1980. 

(d) The suit was, thereafter, transferred to the Court of Munsif (Now Assistant Judge) at Moheshkhali and renumbered there as other Suit No. 189 of 1.984. The suit was again posted for preemptory hearing on 15-5-1984. On that date the plaintiffs-opposite parties were present in the court but the defendants-petitioners defaulted in appearing when the suit was called on hearing. Consequently, the suit was decreed ex parte for the third time on 15-5-1984. The awarding of decree for the third time in favour of the plaintiffs-opposite parties could not deter the defendants-petitioners in proceeding further and took the course of moving the court for restoration of the suit on setting aside ex parte decree on laying a Miscellaneous Case No. 18 of 1985 under Order-9, Rule-13 of the Code of Civil Procedure. With the averments that the defendants-petitioners had not been aware of the date of preemptory hearing and also that the defendant-petitioner No. 1 had been attacked with Peptic Ulcer and had been under the treatment of a doctor. The Miscellaneous case was resisted from the side of plaintiffs-opposite parties on presentation a written objection denying the contentions of the defendants-petitioners made in the Miscellaneous Case. Defendant-petitioner No. 1 examined himself as petitioner witness No. 1 and plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 examined himself as opposite party witness No. 1 in support of respective contentions pleas. The said Miscellaneous Case stood dismissed on 19-5-1985 by the court. The said Order dated 19-5-1985 was set aside by the court of appeal in an appeal being Miscellaneous Appeal No. 224 of 1985 preferred by the defendant petitioners. 

(e) Miscellaneous Case was heard again by the learned Assistant Judge who by the judgment and order dated 10-11-1988 again dismissed it in recording dismissal, the learned Assistant Judge considered pleadings, evidences materials on record, facts and circumstances of the case. The learned Assistant Judge took the view that the Doctor was not examined in support of the alleged illness and a more Medical Certificate was not admissible in evidence. The learned Judge took into account serious laches and negligence on the part of the defendants-petitioners in prosecuting the proceeding and found that the defendants-petitioners for long twenty years took proceeding after proceeding  only to cause harassment to the plaintiffs-opposite parties. 

(f) The defendant-petitioner sought quashing the decisions recorded by the learned Assistant Judge through a medium of appeal being Miscellaneous Appeal No. 53 of 1988 before the learned District Judge, Cox's Bazar. The learned District Judge by the judgment and Order dated I 7.10.1988 dismissed the appeal and maintained decisions rendered by the learned Assistant Judge. The learned Appellate Judge noticed that on four occasions ex parte decree had been awarded in favour of the plaintiffs-opposite parties and on three occasions the suit was restored to its file and number on setting aside the ex parte decrees. The Appellate Judge being last and final Judge of fact rendered positive decision that the defendants-petitioners signally failed to substantiate the plea of existence of sufficient cause for their non-appearance on the date fixed for hearing on account of illness. 

4. Feeling still dissatisfied, the defendants-petitioners approached this court on laying a petition under Section-115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained Rule. 

5. Mr. Abul Kalam Azad, the learned Advocate appeared for the defendants-petitioners. The plaintiffs-opposite parties are rep-resented by Mr. Rabi Sanker Chakrabarty. 

6. The only contention pressed into ser-vice on behalf of the defendants-petitioners is that previous default could not have been taken into consideration by the courts below and the courts below committed a substantial error is refusing to restore that suit taking into consideration the previous defaults of the defendants-petitioners. In support of the said contention reliance has been placed upon Seth Shivrattan G. Mohatta and another Vs Messers Mohammadi Steam Ship Co. Ltd. 17 DLR Sc. 487. 

7. The court's below especially the Court Appeal not only considered previous defaults of the defendant-petitioners but also look into account the failure of the defendants petitioners to prove their alleged illness by examining the doctor. Both the courts below found that the defendant-petitioners failed to substantiate the existence of sufficient cause for non-appearance on the date fixed for hearing on account of illness. True it is that the previous defaults were also considered by the courts below and the courts below rightly considered previous defaults. In Seth Shivrattan C. Mohatta and another Vs. Messers Mohammadi Steam Ship Co. Ltd. 17 DLR Sc. 487, the suit was dismissed for default on First May, 1957 which had been declared Eid Holiday but the court remained open because the moon was not sighted on the previous evening. The Supreme Court of Pakistan stated that by itself constituted a sufficient cause for excusing default in appearance by the plaintiff on that day. The facts and circum-stances of that case in quite distinguish-able in the facts and circumstances of the case in my hand and got no bearing at all. In this context, it is to be borne in mind that a decision is only an authority for what it actually decides, it cannot be quoted for preposition that many seem to follow from it. Every judgment must be read applicable  to the particular facts proved or assumed to  be proved. The generality of expression that  may be found cannot be intended to be exposition of whole law but the same must be regarded as governed or qualified by the  particular facts of the case in which  such expression occur (Emphasis laid). The contention as raised from the side of the defendants petitioner having been devoid of sub-stance stands rejected.

8. True it is that law of procedure is designed to facilitate justice and further its  
ends. It is also true that courts are ordinarily inclined to set  aside ex parte  decree 
unless there been gross default, laches and negligence on the Part of defaulting party.  But it is equally the that gross default  lathes and negligence cannot be condoned where it is manifested that by  that condonation a prejudice and a miscarriage of justice is caused to the other party.  
Every access to justice must not be misused as a licence to a litigant party resorting proceeding after proceeding to have his affairs settled in  the manner he wishes ca using untold harassment to the successful party especially when is a decree holder. No litigant got a right to unlimited 
drought upon court's  valuable  time and  unnecessarily throttle the functioning of justice dispensation system which is self groaning under unbearable arrears and virtually gasping for breath. (Emphasis supplied) 

9. In the case in hand there had been serious defaults, lathes and negligence on 
the part of the defendants-petitioner in prosecuting the proceeding in the court. The courts below considered these defaults, ladies and negligence matter, The courts below also on consideration of pleading, evidence, materials on record, facts and circumstances of the case found that the 
defendants-petitioners failed to substantiate throu0 legal evidence that there had been sufficient cause for their non-appearance in the court when the suit was called on for hearing. On a careful examination of the decisions reasons and conclusion reached by the courts below it cannot be 
said at all that those went against the weight of evidence and materials brought on record and suffer from patent illegality, legal infirmity, perversity and flagrant error of law warranting any interference by this court in the exercises of Civil Revisional Jurisdiction under Section-115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

10. Before parting I am inclined to record my deep appreciation to the learned lawyer 
for the defendants-petitioners Mr. Abul Kalam Azad for presenting the Civil Revision petition 
without mistake of words and sentences which is very rare now-a-days. 

11. No interference is called for?

12. Resultantly, the Rule springing out of Civil Revision Petition having been without any merit -is discharged. 

13. The order of stay granted at the time of issuance of Rule on 11-2-1990 staying ex parte decree dated 15.5.1985 in Other Suit No. 189 of 1984 of the court of Assistant Judge. Moheshkhali, Cox's Bazar stand vacated. 

14. Records be sent down to the courts below at once. 

End.

full_judgment:
Mohammad Fazlul Karim J:- This appeal by leave is directed against the judgment and order dated the 24th day of June, 2003 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 3884 of 1997 making the Rule absolute setting aside the judgment and decree dated 30.04.1997 of the Subordinate Judge-in-Charge, 3rd Court, Mymensingh in Other Class Appeal No. 374 of 1994 reversing those dated 11.10.1994 of the Senior Assistant Judge-in-Charge, Mymensingh Sadar, in Other Class Suit No. 58 of 1993 dismissing the Suit. 

2. The facts involved in the case, in short, are that Sharat Chandra Das, Subash Chandra Das and Satish Chandra Das were the owners of the 0606 acres of land which is the disputed land and that the said land was transferred to Copal Chandra Barman and Norendra Chandra Barman. Copal Chandra Barman built up 2 shops in 0100 acres of land which were given on rent to Idris Ali and Majid Khan. Mozaffar Thlukder became the owner of the shops after the death of his father, Idris Ali that the aforesaid Copal entered into an agreement to sell the land to the plaintiff on 02.07.1973 that on 20.02.1984 Gopal died leaving two sons namely, Bolai and Barun; that Mozaffar Ali, the predecessor of the plaintiff asked Bolai to sell the land to Mozaffar; that the said Bolai having refused the plaintiff filed Other Class Suit No. 366 of 1984. Haji Shull and Hanif appeared in the case with an application for addition of party; that the said application was rejected; that the defendant did not add the plaintiff's predecessor Mozaffar as a party in Other Suit No. 8.1 of 1982 that the plaintiff further stated that they obtained ex-parte decree on 21.07.1985 that on 07.08.1991 the plaintiff got decree for specific performance of contract; executed on 07.08.1991 in execution of the ex-parte decree in their Suit No. 81 of 1982. 

3. The defendant contested the case filing written statement denying material allegations contending, inter-alia, that the plaintiffs suit is barred by limitation; bad for defect of parties and that they obtained the decree by fraud. It is the defendant's claim that the suit land was under the possession of Haji Sharif and Hanif and there was contract for sale of the same dated 26.11.1975 with the owner namely Gopal Chandra Barman Roy. The owner having failed to register the deed of sale, the defendant filed Other Class Suit No. 81 of 1982 for specific performance of contract which was decreed ex-parte on 19.08.1990. The quantum of land claimed by the defendant was 1 arias out of 0606 acres of land of Plot No. 1934. The suit was dismissed; on appeal the same was allowed. The High Court Division made the Rule absolute setting aside the impugned judgment and decree and remanded the case to the Court of Appeal below with a direction to recon-sider its judgment in the light of discussion made in the body of the judgment and to allow the appellant to file an application for partition, if any, and thereafter to dispose of the case in accordance with law. 

4. Leave was granted to consider the submissions of the learned Advocate-on-Record for the appellants that "in view of the suit being one for specific performance of contract, the High Court Division erred in law in remanding the suit to the lower appellate Court in order to enable the respondent to file an application for partition, if any, and dispose of the same in accordance with law, being outside the scope of suit for partition, which would change the nature and character of the suit." 

5. Mr. Md. Nawab Ali, learned Advocate-on-Record, appearing for the appellant submitted that in view of the suit being one for specific performance of contract, the High Court Division erred in law in remanding the suit to the lower appellate Court in order to enable the respondent to file an 'application for partition, if any, and dispose of the same in accordance with law, being outside the scope of suit for partition, which would change the nature and character of the suit. 

6. Mr. Nurul Islam, Bhuiyan, learned Advocate-on-Record, appearing for the respondent submitted that the prayer for declaring the decree dated 19.08.1990 passed in Other Class Suit No. 81 of 1982 in respect of property is void, illegal, collusive and not binding upon the plaintiffs and such prayer comes under Sections 39 and 42 of the Specific Relief Act, and since the defendant claimed possession over the property so the suit is barred by Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. that the decree of the defendants has clouded the title of the plaintiffs over the suit proper but to remove the cloud no prayer has been made for declaration of the title of the plaintiffs over the suit property; that the defendants challenged the possession of the plaintiffs so without a regular suit for declaration of title and recovery/confirmation of possession in the disputed land the plaintiffs cannot challenge the legality of the decree of the defendants. The learned Advocate-on-Record further submitted that the plaintiffs suit for mere declaration is not maintainable without a further prayer for partition and as such, virtually directed .to add a new prayer for partition by amending the plaint; that the suit is barred by limitation inasmuch as the agreement of the defendants with Balal Chandra Barman was entered into on 30.08.1975 and the defendants filed the Other Class Suit No. 366 of 1984 of the plaintiffs stating that they are in possession of the property by virtue of the agreement dated 26.11.1975 and Title Suit No. 81of 198.2 filed by them in the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge is pending; that the predecessor 0.1 the plaintiff, Mozaffar Ali entered into an agreement on 02.07.1973 to purchase the property from Gopal Chandra and continued to pay rent to Gopal Chandra till his death on 20.03.1984 and after his death paid rent to his sons till July, 1984 and thereafter, filed Other Class Suit No. 366 of 1984 and such story is totally unbelievable. 

7. The provisions of Section 12 of the Specific Relief of Contract Act provides that 
(a) when the act agreed be done is in 4, the performance, wholly or partly, of a trust; 
(b) when there exists no standard for ascertaining the actual damage caused by non-performance of the act agreed to be clone; 
(c) when the act agreed to be done is such that pecuniary compensation for is non-performance would not afford adequate relief; or 
(d) when it is probable that pecuniary compensation cannot be got for the., non-performance of the act agreed to be done. 

8. This section contains explanations that unless and until the contrary is proved, the Court shall presume that the breach of a contract to transfer immovable property cannot be adequately relieved by compensation in money and that the breach of a contract to transfer movable property can not be thus, relieved. 

9. From the above, it is crystal clear that a contract may be specifically enforced by way of specific performance, wholly or partly, of a trust on proof of the contract and it is the duty of the Court to enforce the same in its discretion unless the compensation is an adequate relief. 

10. In that view of the matter the petitioner has framed the suit for specific performance of contract under Section 21 of the Specific Relief Act, but in the instant case the High Court Division without considering the frame of the suit for specific performance has directed the suit to he remanded to the lower appellate Court in order, to enable the respondent to file a petition for partition, if any, and to dispose of the suit in accordance with law Obviously, the suit is for specific performance of contract and the plaintiff to get relief within the frame of 'the contract and the fact if proved on evidence, the Court In exercise of its discretion could allow the same or in fitness of the case dismiss the same but could not convert the suit into a suit for partition: which is altogether beyond the scope of specific performance of contract and could not he agitated or disposed of in a suit for specific performance of contract as framed with the averment to that effect inasmuch as a suit for partition is beyond the scope of the suit of specific performance of con-tract and the same would change the nature and character of the suit. It is the cardinal principle of law that the pleading should not be allowed to be amended which would change the nature and character of the pleadings in plaint or written statement. 

11. In the instant case, the High Court Division has remanded the case to the lower appellate Court in order to file an application for partition, if any, and to dispose of the same in accordance with law but the High Court Division has lost sight of the fact that in suit for specific performance of contract if a prayer for partition is incorporated it would introduce totally a different and distinct cause of action and an inconsistent case or cause of action than the original One for which a suit for specific performance of contract was filed or its effect would be to substitute one distinct cause of action for another or to change the nature and character of the suit and as such, such direction was not permissible in law or is not legally tenable within the frame of the suit for specific performance of contract. 

12. In a suit for specific performance of contract the cause of action is the agreement, oral and documentary, to transfer the particular property but the suit for partition would be a suit for partition among co-sharers on the basis their rights in the cjmali or joint properties which is altogether a different and inconsistent cause of action for which the suit for specific performance in respect of particular agreement to transfer of any property has been filed and thus, a completely inconsistent or contrary plca/cause of action and subject matter which could not he allowed to be introduced in the suit or on a fresh plea/pleas. Such plea/pleas would be contrary or inconsistent with the plea of the plaint in a suit for specific performance of contract for specific relief in the suit. 

13. In the case of Kandu and others-vs. Woghu 3 DLR (PC) 310 it has been held that the determination in a cause should be founded upon a case to be found in the pleadings or involved in or consistent with the case thereby made. Therefore, the District Judge in appeal, framed a new issue which did not arose on the pleading, he acted wrongly." 

14. Furthermore, though Order 6 Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure conferred upon the Court a very wide power but it must he exercised in accordance with legal principles. Thus, under no circumstances, it could involve the setting up of a newer case. In a case of Ma Shere Mye-vs-Maung Mothkaugn reported in (3) L.R. 48 & A 217 Lord A Buck. Master held that it was not open to a Court under Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure to allow amendment which altered the real matter in controversy between the parties. 

15. In that view of the matter, we hold that the direction of the High Court Division to the effect that "remanding the suit to the lower appellate Court to file an application for partition, if any, or to dispose of the same in accordance with law" would accordingly he beyond the scope of suit for specific performance of contract and the same would change the nature and character of the suit and in that view of the matter the order of remand must be held to be illegal and is liable to be set aside. 

16. Accordingly, the impugned order of remand is set aside and the Appellate Court is directed to dispose of the appeal in accordance with law. 

17. This appeal is, accordingly, allowed without any order as costs. 

End.
