Mr. Mohammad Abdur Rashid, J: Defendant No. 1 to 3 presented the above first appeal against judgment and decree dated 23.01.02 passed by learned Joint District Judge, Second Commercial Court and Artha Rin Adalat at Chittagong in other Suit No. 19 of 1993, which decreed the suit as prayed for partition. 

2. Originally, respondent No. 1 to 3 and Saleha Khatun as plaintiffs instituted the suit for partition for a share of about 6.95 acres of land against the appellants and others and also for declaration that the deed of gift dated 25.08.84 in favour of the defendant No. 1 was forged, fraudulent, false and not binding upon the plaintiffs. 

3. Plaint case, in short, is that Bacha Mia, predecessor-in-interest of both plaintiffs and defendants had three wives namely, Asaba, Chunni and Parijan. He had two sons, Saleh and Munshi and four daughyers, namely, Asma, Kulsuma, Hazera and Siraja Khatun by Asaba; one daughter Golbahar by Chunni and another daughter Saleha by Parijan. All his three wives died during his lifetime. 

4. In 1959, son Munshi died leaving one son Anwarul Azim and two daughters, namely Anwara and Laila, who are defendant no. 1 to 3. In 1960, daughter Siraja Khatun died leaving two sons, namely, Mahbub and Nurul and one daughter Jernha, defendant no, 13 to 15. on 31.08.68 Bacha Mia Died. Golbahar died leaving three daughters namely, Fatema, Anowara and Zohra who are planti ff No. 2 to 4. Hazera died leaving two sons, namely, Ezhar and Rafiz and two daughters, namely, Halima and Golbahar, defendant no. 8 to 11. Saleh died on 03.08.84 issueless leaving 2 wives, namely, Amira arid Sobura who are defendant No. 4 and 5 and 2 sisters namely Asma and Kulsuma, defendant No. 6 and 7. During the pendency of the suit, defendant no. 7 Asma died leaving 2 sons, namely, Salam and Malek, one daughter Rabeya and grandchildren by another daughter Sakhina. Said 2 sons and  1 daughter were ultimately added as plaintiff No. 6 to 8 while the grandchildren by Sakhina as defendant No. 16 to 
24. 
5. It further appears that Saleha daughter of Parijan who was originally plaintiff No. 1 was then transposed as defendant No. 25 and defendant No. 5 Sabura wife of Saleh as plaintiff No. 5 Ultimately plaintiff No. 2 to 8 prosecuted the suit. 

6. Further case of the plaintiffs, in short, is that during the lifetime of their father Saleh and Munshi acquired 3.73 acres of land, which is described into schedule la' to the plaint. Each of the brothers became owner in possession of 1.865 acres of land. After death of Munshi, his father Bacha Mia got 0.31 acre of land and defendant No. 1 to 3 as sole legal representatives acquired the rest of said 1.865 acres of land. 

7. The property described in schedule 'Kha' was the self acquired property of Bacha Mia. Defendant No. 1 Anowarul Azim got the land by way of gift described in schedule 'Ga'. The property described in schedule 'Gha' was the self acquired property of deceased Saleh Ahmed. 

8. Besides, when elder brother Munshi died leaving two minor sons and one daughter, Saleh Ahmed took care of them. He had no children of his own. He raised them as his own. He got married defendant no. 1 and gave marriage to defendant no. 3. He ultimately gave the management of his property to defendant no. 1. Within 22 days of his death, defendant no. 1 got a deed of gift executed and registered by Amira and Sabura, two wives and two surviving sisters Asma and Kulsuma by false representation which was shown witnessed and written by a scribe of different villages in order to grab the property left by Saleh Ahmed by depriving all his legal representatives. 

9. Said four illiterate and 'Pardanashin' village women never intended to gift their land 
to the defendant No. 1 nor gifted and delivered possession of the land covered by the gift. Lastly, on 31.01.86 lastly the plaintiffs demanded for partition, which was refused. Hence, the suit. 

10. Defendant No. I to 3 contested the suit by filing a joint written statement. In the written statement, the genealogy as given in the plaint was not disputed. Their main case, in short, is that during the lifetime, Saleh Ahmed desired and asked his heirs, particularly, his two wives Amira and Sabora and two sisters Asma and Kulsuma to gift their entire shares to defendant No. 1 if he could not carry out his due to illness. Ultimately, Saleh Ahmed could not carry out his wish. After his death; said wives and sisters jointly executed and registered a deed of gift dated 25.08.84 giving their entire shares in the land left by Saleh Ahmed to the defendant. 

11. They also claimed that Saleha defendant no. 25 (originally, plaintiff No. 1) and Gulbahar, predecessor-in-interest of plaintiff no. 2 to 4 also orally gifted their entire shared which they inherited to defendant no. 1. The plaintiffs had no possession or title in any property in the suit and as such, the suit was liable to be dismissed. 

12. Defendant No. 4 Amira and 6 Kulsuma filed a joint written statement supporting the case of defendant No. 1 to 3 but ultimately never turned up in Court to support their written statement. 

13. Defendant No. 5 and 7 filed two separate written statements mainly denying the execution and registration of deed of gift and giving any land to defendant no. 1 by way of gift. Defendant No. 5 Sabura deposed in support of her written statement as PW-2 and also prayed for a 'Saham' while defendant No. 7 died' before the trial. 

14. On the pleadings the issues settled include: whether the suit was maintainable in the manner and form framed; defect of parties; barred by limitation; entire joint property brought to the hotch pot and the deed of gin being No. 171 I dated 25.08.84 was collusive, illegal, forged and ineffective; and as to what right or title the plaintiffs were entitled to for partition. 

15. The plaintiffs examined two witnesses while the defendants examined three witnesses. The documents adduced by the plaintiffs were marked as Exhibit 1 to 5 series while those of the defendants marked as Exhibit 'Ka' to 'ha'. 

16. Learned Joint District Judge found that the deed of gift dated 25.08.84 was forged, fraudulent, illegal and in effective and that defendant no. 1 acquired no title by such gift and that the story of oral gifts as claimed by defendant no. 1 were also all false. He however rejected the case of plaintiffs with regard to the share certificates in Bangladesh Oxygen Limited. 

17. Upon such view, learned Joint District Judge decreed the suit declaring the deed of gift being No. 1711 dated 25.08.84 illegal, collusive, void and ineffective and that the defendant No. I had acquired no title or interest by such gift; and allotting a share of 06.65 acres to the plaintiffs out of schedule-'Ka', 'Kha', 'Ga' and 'Gha' to the plaint. 

18. Mr. Hasnat Quayum, learned advocate for the appellant took us through the record and submitted that when the plaintiffs particularly plaintiff No. 5 Sabura having admitted execution and registration of the deed of gift dated 25.08.84 in dock the learned Joint District Judge was wrong to hold that the defendants failed to prove that the deed of gift was genuine. 

19. He submitted that plaintiff No. 2 to 4 were neither donors nor claimed any interest through any of the donors, so they were not entitled to challenge the deed of gift in the suit. Similarly, plaintiff No. 5 to 8 were transposed on 17.02.92 and as such, the relief of declaration against the deed of gift was barred by limitation on that day so far they were concerned. 

20. Lastly, he submitted that defendant No. 1 has proved the execution and registration of the deed of gift, and he was admittedly on possession of the land and plaintiffs could not deny their LTIs on the deed, and the learned Joint District Judge fell in serious error in declaring said deed of gift collusive and forged. 

21. On the other hand, Mr. Mahbubay Alam, learned senior Advocate however submitted that Saleh Ahmed died on o3.08.84 and within 22 days of his death on. 25.05.84 there was no reason for his legal representatives to give away their entire interest to defendant No. 1 only.

 22. He submitted that after death of Saleh Ahmed, his two wives and two sisters became wholly depended upon defendant No. 1. Taking the advantage of their helpless conditions, defendant no. I obtained their LT's on blank papers saying those were necessary for withdrawal of money from the bank left by Saleh Ahmed and brought into existence said deed of gift with those papers. 

23. He submitted that defendant no. 1 also admitted that said wives and sisters were illiterate and 'Pardanashin' and they made application for succession certificate and he looked after the case as Tadbirkar'. In the circumstances, he submitted that the learned Joint District Judge correctly found that the deed of gift was a product of forgery. 

24. Lastly, he submitted that said defendants having failed to prove that alleged donors actually ever intended and expressed their intention to gift and gifted their entire shares to defendant No. 1 and delivered possession, the conclusion of learned Joint District Judge that the gift was collusive and forged does not call for any interference.

25. In support, he cited Siddique Ahmed and others Vs Gani Ahmed and others, (I 981) 33 DLR (AD) 1 and Rokeya Khatun Vs Alijan, (1982) 32 DLR (AD) 266. 

26. We have perused the record. 

27. We found no dispute among the parties with regard to the genealogy. Nor with regard to the decision on hotch pot, defect of parties etc. The appellants also could not press the appeal on the acquisition of any property by defendant no. 1 by way of oral gifts from Saleha, defendant no. 25 (original plaintiff no. I) and Gulbahar, predecessor of plaintiff no. 2 to 4 as they failed to adduce any evidence whatsoever on such oral gifts. So, the entitlement of said Saleha through
her mother Parijan and plaintiff no. 2 to 4 through their mother Gulbahar in the property left by Bacha Miah was correctly found by the learned Joint District Judge to be established. 

28. Learned advocate for the appellants did not deny the position that if the conclusion of the learned Joint District Judge on the deed of gift dated 25.08.84 could not be dislodged then the allotment of shares as made him would not suffer any change. So, only issue facing us in this appeal is whether the learned Joint District Judge was well founded in disbelieving and disregarding the deed of gift dated 25.08.84 from his consideration. 

29. In respect of deed of gift Abdul Malek as PW-1 as attorney of plaintiff no. 2 to 4 deposed that the deed of gift dated 25.08.84 was forged, ineffective and fraudulent. Defendant No. 4, 5, 6 and 7 all were illiterate, old and 'Pardanisin' village women. They had no idea about the deed of gift. Defendant No. 1 never expressed to any body about the gift. The deed of gift was brought into existence within 22 days of death of Saleh Ahmed. The deed of gift was never acted upon. The defendant No. 1 also never put in the original deed of gift till date. The scribe and witnesses to the said deed of gift had no reason to know said four women as they were of different villages. Said four women never executed nor registered said deed of gift. The deed of gift was never read over and explained to said four women, nor shown to them before execution and registration. Said women never gifted nor delivered possession of the land they inherited. After taking a copy of the deed of gift, they came to know that by said deed 10.12 acres of land was shown to have been gifted. Said four women had no authority or title to transfer so much land. Defendant No. 1 was a clever educated businessman and also a contractor. The plaintiffs were in possession through 'bargader' of the land of plot No. 4105, 4111. Defendant NO. 5 examined himself as PW-2. 

30. He stated that Munshi Miah died leaving defendant no. 1 as child. Saleh Ahmed no 
children. He raised defendant 1 as his own child, gave him proper education and ultimately, entrusted him with his property when he could not manage his property due to old age. Saleh Ahmed got defendant no. 1 and 2 married. Said four helpless women never knew the scribe or the witnesses of the deed who were of different villages. 

31. Sabura Khatun, plaintiff no. 5 (originally defendant no. 5) deposed as PW-2 that she was the second wife of deceased Saleh Ahmed. She testified that she and defendant no. 6 and 7 had never any intention to gift the land she inherited from her husband and they inherited from their brother. On 25.08.84 they never executed any deed of gift by putting their LTI's nor did they go to sub-registry office. Defendant no. 1 never told them about any gift of any property. They never asked the scribe to write the deed. The deed of gift was never read over to them. They never put LTIs on any deed of gift. They never asked any body to witness a deed of gift. They were in possession of their land. They duly gave power to PW-1 Abdul Malek to prosecute the case on their behalf. 

32. In cross-examination, she said that she was given in marriage 40/45 years ago, when defendant no. 1 was not born. They were in one family. They brought up defendant no. 1. She used to love him as her own child. At the time of death, her husband did not tell her anything. She stated that defendant No. 1 was behaving well so long her husband was alive. After his death, he turned into bad. 

33. In the house of the defendant No. I their LTIs were taken saying for making application. When they gave LTI he did not go to the grave of her husband. She knew DW-2 Mahbub Ali and he was husband of Siraja Khatun, sister of her husband. She transferred 1 kani land to the wife of defendant No. 1. She had possession in her possession. Then, she said defendant No. I forcibly was enjoying. When, they refused to give LTIs they were driven out of the house. Defendant no 1 obtained her LTI saying for obtaining loan from the bank. It was not true that she voluntarily executed the 'Kabala' by putting LTI. She reiterated that she never asked the scribe write the deed of gift. She denied that the deed was read over to them. She could say that LTIs were taken but could not say what happened thereafter. 

34. On the other hand, Defendant No. 1 deposed that Saleh Ahmed had no issue. During his old age sickness, he wished and asked his heirs to make a gift of their land to Defendant No. 1. Saleh Ahmed raised as a son and he was living with him in the same family and looking after them. After the death of Shleh Ahmed, his two wives Amira and Sabura and two daughters Kulsuma and Asma in carrying out his wish on 25.08.84 executed and registered the deed of gift being No. 1711 Exhibit-'Chha'. Pursuant to the gift, he got possession of the gifted land. After the deed of gift, by cutting earth and rearing fish he possessed the land. He stated that it was not true that he created the deed of gift after taking their LTIs saying for taking loan from the bank. He however did not say a word about his story of oral gifts at all Saleha and Gulbahar. 

35. In cross-examination, he said that two wives and two sisters of late Saleh Ahmed made an application for a succession certificate for withdrawal of money from bank left by him. They four were illiterate and 'Pardanashin' women. He looked after the case as 'Tadbirkar'. He obtained the succession certificate and they withdrew money with the help of said certificate. (The certificate was not however adduced.) He denied that taking LTIs for the succession certificate he created the forged and fabricated deed of gift in collusion with the scribe and witnesses. 

36. DW-2 Mahbub Alam deposed that on 25.08.84 Amira and others executed and registered the deed of sale. The donors executed the deed by putting their LTIs. He identified them and took their KTIs in the office of sub-register. He also identified his signature.

37. In cross-examination, he said that the deed was written in the house of defendant rro. of the witnesses, Dipok and Jane Alam went to the house and other witnesses went to the office of sub-registrar. Writing commenced at 8/8.30 AM and completed at 11/11.30 Am. Donors put their LTIS at the office of sub-registrar. All of the witnesses put signatures at the office of sub-registrar. He had some education. He could not remember on how many pages how many signatures were taken. Siraja Khatun, mother of defendant no. 13 to 14 was his mother. He said that he did not know that he was defendant no. 13 in the suit. He denied that getting huge money from defendant no. 1 he deposed falsely. 

38. DW-3 Dipok deposed that he knew the donors and donee of the registered deed of gift being No. 1711 dated 25.08.84.He witnessed to the gift. He also identified his signature. The scribe of the gift Nirmal Kanti Dey was his uncle. He was sick at the time. The donors executed the deed by putting their LTIs in front of him. Mr. Mahbub Alam signed their names on their behalf. It may be noted that he did not however identify the signature of the scribe. 

39. In cross-examination, he said that sitting in the Fatehbad sub-registry office, he signed the deed as a witness. Donors were 'Pardanisin' muslim women. If the donors came before him, he could identify them. He said that Asma Khatun was Anowarul Azim's brother's daughter. (In fact, Asma was sister of Saleh Ahmed.) He denied that the witnesses and Anowarul Azim (defendant no. 1) created the deed in collusion with each other, that the donors never went to the sub-registrar office and that they did never executed and register the deed. He also denied that Nirmal Kanti Dey was not sick and he did not come, as he could not tell a lie. 

40. None of defendant no. 4 Amira Khatun and no. 6 Kulsuma turned up to depose in support of their written statement. 

41. That is all the evidence for and against execution and registration of the deed of gift on 'record. It appears from the record that plaintiff no. 5 Sabura Kahtun admitted to have given some LTIs. But she deposed that their LTIs were taken by defendant no. 1 for making application for withdrawal of money from bank. Defendant no. 1 as DW-1 admitted that said four donors were illiterate and 'Pardanashin' village women. He looked after their case for succession certificate as a 'Tadbirkar'. 

42. Defendant no. I stated that Shleh Ahmed raised him as a son as he had no children. He got education living in the family of Saleh Ahmed. When, Shleh Ahmed became old he managed his property. He claimed that during his lifetime Saleh Ahmed desired to transfer his entire land to him by way of gift but due to sickness he could not do so. Before death, Saleh Ahmed asked all his heirs to make a gift of their entire shares in his land to the defendant no. 1 if he ultimately could not make the gift. But said defendant could not find anyone to corroborate him on such wish or desire of Saleh Ahmed. Rather, the circumstances as borne out by the record clearly indicate that at the time, 22 days after the death of Saleh Ahmed, all of alleged donors had to be depended upon the defendant no. 1. They became old by the time. 

43. The deed of gift was exhibited as Exhibit-'Ccha'. None of witnesses of the defence witnesses could have testified that before the LTIs were taken the deed was read over and explained to any of said four donors; and having understood the contents and purport of the deed they executed the deed by putting their LTIs on the said deed. None of the relations of said donors was present to witness the deed of gift nor had any say in the matter nor came to support' the defendants. The scribe of deed was also not examined. After the death of Saleh Ahmed, when defendant No. I took their LTIs, said women could not be claimed to be not in their bereavement. 

44. It is true when LTIs on a document are admitted the author of such LT1s is required to prove the circumstances in which the document was brought into existence. Registration of a document also raises a presumption of regularity. But the above circumstances as brought on record sufficiently rebutted the presumption and shifted the onus on the defendant no. I to prove that said women executed and registered the deed of gift giving up their entire shares to him. 

45. It is also true that all the donors are illiterate, 'Pardanashi' old Muslim village women. On the other hand, defendant No. 1 was an educated businessman. He was living with defendant no. 4 Saleha Khatun and plaintiff no. 5 Sabura Khatun and managing the property left by Saleh Ahmed. His position in the family and relation with the four illiterate and 'Pardanashin' women cannot be ignored from consideration. 

46. A special rule of onus was devised in the sub-continent to protect certain category of women who suffer from some disabilities and disadvantages because of 'pardah' system. It applies to all 'pardahnashin' women, literate or illiterate. Then, the protection was extended to ignorant and illiterate woman though not strictly 'pardahnashin'. Secondly, in a case when transfer by a 'pardahnashin' woman is denied by s such women, the onus is always on the party wk. want, to hold such women to the terms of the deed to satisfy the Court by evidence that she substantially understood the disposition and she executed the deed with full understanding of what she doing and of the nature and effect of the transaction. Thirdly, when the transferee or donee stands in a position of active confidence or had fiduciary relationship with the 'pardahnashin' woman he carries additional burden to prove that such woman had independent and disinterested advice from persons other than the recipient of the document in executing a deed; cf: Siddique Ahmed V Gani Ahmed, (1981) 33 DLR (AD) 01 and 

47. In the facts and circumstances of the case, the defendants-appellant hopelessly failed to discharge any of the special onuses, as stated above. All the alleged vendors were illiterate and 'Pardahnashin' village women. On the evidence, it is clear that defendant no. 1 was in a position of active confidence with said women. Defendants failed to prove that said women had any independent advice from anybody before the execution of the deed of gift and they understood the disposition and having understood the contents of the deed executed the deed. 

48. Besides, where a deed of gift is challenged the donee under the gift is not exempted from proving the essential ingredients of a gift by a Muslim, namely, offer and acceptance of the gift and delivery of possession of land covered by gift. 

49. We find no evidence at all adduced by said defendants that said alleged vendors ever offered or desired to make a gift of the land defendant No. 1 and defendant No. 1 accepted the gift and that pursuant to the gift, they delivered the possession to defendant No. 1 which he also accepted. He also failed to prove that the land measuring about 12.10 acres shown to be covered by the gift exclusively belonged to said four women. 

50. Moreover, the learned Joint District Judge mentioned number of reasons for said women in not making gift of their entire interest in favour of defendant no. 1 only. We find no earthly reason for defendant No. 4, 5, 6 and 7 intended to exclude their heirs from inheritance in order to benefit defendant No.1 only and even to deny their own interest executed the deed transferring their entire interest. 

51. Lastly, fraud vitiates everything. When a gift is found to be forged and fraudulent, it is the duty of the court to get rid of such deed from the record. 

52. In the circumstances, we find learned Joint District Judge committed no error in holding that the deed of gift was forged, fraudulent and ineffective; and that defendant No. 1 acquired no title by such gift. The appeal, therefore, has got no merit. 

53. In the result, the appeal is dismissed with cost. Impugned judgment and decree are hereby affirmed. Let the connected Rule being No. 128(f) of 2002 be also discharged with cost. Order of stay granted at the time of issue of the Rule on 17.04.02 is hereby recalled and vacated.
 
54. Send down the LCR at once. 

End.

Mr. Gour Gopal Saha, J. : This rule is directed against the order dated 6.4.97 passed by the learned 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Barisal in Title Suit No. 255 of 1974 setting aside the ex parte decree dated 2.3.75 under Section-5 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

2. No one appears to press the rule.

3. Mr. Md. Altaf Hossain Khan, the learned Deputy Attorney General appearing for the Government of Bangladesh, opposes the rule and prays for discharging the rule on merit.

4. In view of the fact that this is a pretty old case arising out of an order, we are inclined to dispose it of on merit on the basis of materials on record.

5. Short facts relevant for the purpose of the case are that the petitioners as plaintiffs instituted a suit in the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Barisal being Title Suit No. 255 of 1974, praying for declaration of title in the suit property covering an area of 370.70 acres of land. The plaintiffs claimed the suit property on the basis of an oral settlement by the ex-landlords. In the suit the Govt. of Bangladesh appears to have been made defendant No. 108. The suit was eventually decreed on compromise on 1.1.75 within 3 months of filing of the suit.

6. On coming to learn about the aforesaid compromise decree, the Government of Bangladesh filed an application before the learned Subordinate Judge, Barisal stating inter alia that no summons was served upon it and on fraudulent suppression of material facts and by practicing fraud upon the Court the cunning plaintiffs obtained a collusive compromise decree causing heavy losses to it. It appears that the Government of Bangladesh initially filed an application under order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the disputed compromise decree dated 1.1.75. Thereafter an application on behalf of defendant-Government of Bangladesh was failed under Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the collusive decree on the ground of fraud. It has been alleged that the disputed collusive comprise decree was passed by the learned Sub-ordinate Judge without properly applying his judicial mind into facts and circumstances of the case. It is alleged that the plaintiffs had represented to the Court that all the defendants, including the Govt. of Bangladesh, were parties to the compromise petition and on such misrepresentation the plaintiffs obtained the disputed compromise decree causing incalculable losses to the Government.

7. The learned Subordinate Judge after carefully going through the case record, the order sheet of the case and the submissions of the contending parties clearly, found that the plaintiffs by practicing fraud upon the Court obtained the disputed compromise decree. The learned Subordinate Judge was also good enough to find that the Court itself was in error in accepting the false representation of the plaintiffs that all the defendants, including the Govt. were signatories to the compromise petition, although no notice was served upon the Govt. of Bangladesh and it never appeared before the Court to sign to so-called compromise petition. It is found from the order book that no summons was even issued to the Government of Bangladesh, not to speak of serving any summons upon it. In such view of the matter, it is abundantly clear the learned Subordinate Judge was obviously misled by the false representation made by the plaintiffs in stealing the fraudulent compromise decree behind the back beyond the knowledge of their defendant Govt. of Bangladesh causing it serious prejudice.

8. The main ground on which this application has been founded is that since the Government of Bangladesh earlier filed an application under Order-9 Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure the learned Subordinate Judge acted illegally in giving the defendant the relief under Section-151 of the Code of Civil Procedure in exercise of its inherent power. We have carefully gone through the impugned order and the materials on record. It is an undisputed fact that the disputed compromise decree was obtained by the plaintiff-petitioners within 3 months of filing of the suit involving 109 defendants, including the Government of Bangladesh, in the suit. It has been clearly found by the learned Subordinate Judge that the Government of Bangladesh was not a party to the compromise petition, on which the decree was passed. It has already been found that even no notice was issued to the defendant government. It is thus evident that the disputed ex parte compromise decree was obtained by the plaintiff-petitioners by practicing fraud upon the Court. The learned Subordinate Judge was palpably misled by the misrepresentations made by the designing plaintiffs in passing the compromise decree and the learned Subordinate Judge made no protections in admitting its own fault in passing the compromise decree under challenge.

<u>9. It is true, ordinarily the Court does not exercise its inherent power under Section-151 of the Code of Civil Procedure whenever a remedy is available to the aggrieved party under any provision of the Code of Civil Procedure. But; it is also well-settled that if the disputed order or decree is obtained by a party by practicing fraud upon the Court or it has been occasioned due to the fault of the Court or Court officials, the Court has not only the competence in exercise of its inherent power under Section 151 of the Code to undo the wrong done to the aggrieved party but also it is imperative in the interest of justice to do so. Fraud always vitiates all solemn transactions and a fraudulent act by its own nature is a nullity in the eye of law and it is never protected by law. In such cases it will be highly inequitable and in just to ask the wronged party to seek his relief under other ardous is and time consuming provisions of law instead of giving him a relief under 151 of the Code as the special preserve of the Court for doing justice. It deserves to be noted in this connection that procedures are just means towards advancement of the cause of justice and not certainly for obstructing it in the name of technical fall-outs. The filing of an application under Order 9 Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure cannot be allowed to stand in the way of the relief the defrauded defendant is entitled to under the law. We are satisfied in the facts of the case, that the learned Subordinate Judge rightly exercised his power under Section-151 of the Code in giving the appropriate relief to the wronged. We find no merit in the case which fails accordingly.</u>

10. In the result, the rule is discharged without as order as to cost and the impugned order dated 3.3.97 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Barisal in Title Suit No. 255 of 1974 is affirmed.

11. The order of stay granted earlier by this Court is hereby vacated.

12. The suit was filed as back as in the year 1974. It is by now 25 years of old. It is absolutely necessary in the interest of justice that it be disposed of with utmost expediency. The learned Subordinate Judge, Barisal is directed to dispose of the suit within 6 months of the receipt of this order, with due notice to the contending parties.

13. Communicate this order to the learned Subordinate Judge, Barisal at once.

End.

Sreemati Sobita Rani Bonik ----- Petitioner
Versus
Sree Gouranga Prasad Acharjee & Ors ----- Opposite parties
full_judgment:
Mr. Borhanuddin, J:- This rule has been issued calling upon the plaintiff-opposite party No.1 to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 19.08.2004 and 26.08.2004 respectively passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Additional Court, Chittagong in Other Appeal No. 132 of 2004 allowing appeal partially setting aside the judgment and decree dated 29.02.2004 and 06.03.2004 respectively passed by the learned Assistant Judge, In-charge, Boalkhali Upazilla Court, Chittagong in Other Suit No. 96 of 2001 preliminary decreeing the suit in part should not be set aside and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

2. Facts necessary for disposal of the Rule are that the opposite party No. I as plaintiff filed other Suit No.96 of 2001 for partition of the schedule 1 land along with a prayer for direction of sale of the schedule 2 property to the plaintiff according to the provision of Section 4 of the partition Act, 1893, contending that the property appertaining R.S. Khatian No. 3005 originally belonged to Shema Kumaree and Shama Kumaree who sold the said property to Upendra and others and to Brajabala by 2(two) separate kabalas dated 29.03.1935 and 23.06.1943 respectively. The said Upendra and Brajabala sold their shares to Charubala vide two registered kabalas dated 24.02.1949 and 15.02.1949 respectively. After the death of Charubala her shares devolved upon her 4 sons namely; (i) Sachindra, (ii) Ratan, (iii) Anil (iv) Jitendra and 3 daughters namely; (i) Rani, (ii) Sabita, (iii) Anima and husband Ramani. Said Ramani, Sachidra and Anil sold the suit schedule 1 land to the plaintiff vide 2 separate kabalas dated 13.02.1985 and 14.10.1988 respectively. Suit schedule I is a dwelling house wherein the plaintiff has been residing. The defendant Nos.2-4 sold their shares to defendant No.1 which is adjacent to north portion of the plaintiffs dwelling house and as such the plaintiff is entitled to Purchase the said land through Court from defendant No. 1 who is a stranger and not a member of the undivided family. Though the suit land is ejmali with the defendants but the plaintiff is facing difficulty to live peacefully and as such he demanded amicable partition but the defendants refused to do so and the defendant No.1 refused to sell the land of the suit schedule 2 to the plaintiff hence the plaintiff constrained to file the suit. 

3. The defendant No.1 contested the suit by filing written statement. He admits that Charubala was the original owner of the suit land by purchase and on her death her property devolved upon her 4 sons and 3 daughters. He further stated that the defendant Nos.2-4 sold 6 decimals of land appertaining to suit khatian to the defendant No.1 by bringing the defendant No.1 by bringing this fact of transfer to the notice of the plaintiff on 23.01.1991. He emphatically stated that the Plaintiff has no necessity of the suit schedule land and the claim of the Plaintiff is false and such prayed for dismissal of the suit. 

4. This Petitioner as defendant No.4 contested the suit by filing written statement contending that the suit schedule property is the stridhan of Charubala who purchased it by her own and on her death her said Property being Stridhan devolved upon her 4 sons and 3 daughter but not upon her husband and as such the plaintiffs claim by way of purchase from the husband of Charubala has no legal basis. The defendant No. 1 after purchasing the land from defendant nos.2-4 executed a contract for sale of the same in favour of defendant No.4 on 03.03.1997 and delivered possession and Pursuant to that contract sold the said land to the defendant No.4 vide kabala dated 20.05.2003. She further contended that the plaintiff being not a member of the undivided family of Sachindra is not entitled to purchase the land as prayed for and as such prayed for dismissal of the suit. 

5. During trial of the suit the plaintiff himself adduced evidence as P.W. I and 2 more witnesses also adduced evidence in support of the plaint case and on behalf of the defendant No.4, her husband deposed as D.W.1 and one more witness adduced evidence in support of the case of defendant No.4 and both the parties produced their respective documents to prove their respective cases. 

6. After conclusion of trial of the suit the trial court decreed the suit in part in the preliminary form allotting saham to the plaintiff to the tune of 07 decimals of land by way of partition vide judgment and decree dated 29.02.2004 and 06.03.2004 respectively. 

7. Being aggrieved by the judgment and decree of the trial court the plaintiff as appellant preferred Other Appeal No. 132 of 2004 before the District Judge, Additional Court, Chittagong. After filing of the appeal on 15.04.2004, the same was allowed within 4 months by exparte judgment, and decree dated 19.08.2004 and 26.08.2004 respectively. 

8. Mr. Shishir Kanti Majumder, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant No. 4-petitioner appraised the judgment of the trial court and also the judgment of the Court of appeal and also appraised the evidences adduced by both the parties. He submits that the suit was filed for partition and buyup under section 4 of the Partition Act and the plaintiff- appellant-opposite party No.1 being not a member of the undivided family is not entitled to get relief under section 4 of the Partition Act. He next submits that the defendant No.4 petitioner categorically stated in her written statement that the suit property is the Siridhan of Charubala who purchased the same in her name by her own and the D.W. No.1 in his examination-in-chief also Corroborated the Statement made in the written statement which was not Controverted by the plaintiff in any manner. He also submits that the findings of the trial Court did not reverse by the Court of appeal. He further submits that the Appellate Court did not discuss the evidences as adduced by the respective parties. In support of his submission Mr. Majumder referred the case of Santosh Kr. Mitra Vs. Kalipada Das and others reported in AIR 1981 (Cal) 278; the case of Khanderao Dattatraya Wakde Vs. Balkrishna Mahalew Phulambrikar and others reported in AIR 1922 (Bombay) 121 and also the case of Alekha Mantri Vs. Jagabandhu Mantri and others reported in AIR 1971 (Urisha) 127. 

9. Mr. Tahan Kanti Das, the learned Advocate entered appearance on behalf of the plaintiff-opposite party No.1 by filing power but did not file any Counter-affidavit. He submits that the contention of the Stridhan is not proved. He also submits that after marriage the defendant No.4-petitioner is not a member of the undivided family. He further submits that the opposite party No.1 is residing in the suit Plot by way of earlier purchase and as such there is no scope to treat him as stranger in the suit schedule land.

10. Heard the learned Advocates of the respective parties at length, perused the revisional application along with annexures appended thereof and also the Lower Court's Record exhibits, deposition and the decisions referred by the learned Advocate for the petitioner and also the provisions of law. 

11. I have carefully gone through the judgment passed by the trial Court and also tile Court of appeal. The opposite party No.1 as Plaintiff filed Suit for partition of the suit schedule I Property along with a Prayer for direction of sale of the Suit schedule 2 Property under the Provision of Section 4 of the Partition Act. 1893. Section 4 of the Partition Act runs as follows: 
"(1) Where a share of a dwelling-house belonging to an undivided family has been transferred to a person who is not a member of such family and such transferee sues for partition, the Court shall, if any member of the family being a share-holder shall undertake to buy the share of such transferee, make a valuation of such share in such manner as it thinks fit and direct the sale of such share to such share-holder, and may give all necessary and proper directions in that behalf. 
(2) If in any case described in sub-section (1) two or more members of the family being such share-holders severally undertake to buy such share, the Court shall follow the procedure prescribed by sub-section (2) of the last foregoing section." 
By now it is settled by law that under the Provision of Section 4 of the Partition Act. "family" includes a group of persons related by blood. Admittedly vendors of the kabala dated 23.01.91 i.e. defendant nos. 2-4 are not persons or group of persons related by blood to the plaintiff and as such the suit land alleged to be adjacent to -the dwelling-house of the plaintiff is not found belonging to the undivided family of the plaintiff. The defendant No. I did not purchase the share of a dwelling-house belonging to an undivided family of the Plaintiff which is a condition in order to enable the plaintiff to have a direction of sell under section 4 of the Partition Act, 1893. The trial Court rightly observed that the plaintiff vide kabala dated 13.02.85 and 14.10.88 respectively became a share holder of the suit khatian but did not become a member of the undivided family of the vendors pursuant to the said kabalas and as such the prayer for direction of sale of the schedule 2 land to the plaintiff is not in accordance with law. In reversing the findings of the trial Court the learned joint District judge quoted a portion of the judgment of the Supreme Court. The relevant Portion is reproduced below: 
"এই ক্ষেত্রে মহামান্য হাইকোর্ট সিভিল রিভিশন ৭৩৩,১৯৯৮ মামলার মহামান্য সুপ্রীমকোর্টের আপীল বিভাগে আদেশের অংশ বিশেষ উদ্ধৃতকরা হইল।(sic) 

"The main purpose behind enacting Section 4 is to Protect and Preserve the co-sharers sentiment and attachment to their ancestral house and also to Preserve Pardah and privacy of the members in inmates of the undivided dwelling house. It is further held in this case that a Co-sharers prayer to buy up a stranger Purchaser may not be refused on technical ground" From plaint reading of the quoted paragraph, it appears that the very purpose of Section 4 is to protect and preserve the sentiment of the co-sharers and attachment to their ancestral property and also preserve the privacy of the members of the undivided family. I failed to understand by quoting the aforesaid paragraph how the lower Appellate Court came to a conclusion the plaintiff appellant is entitled to buy up under section 4 of the Partition Act. Under the aforesaid facts I subscribe The view of the trial Court that since the plaintiff appellant-opposite party is not a member of the undivided family as such his prayer for buy up under Section 4 of the Partition Act is not sustainable in law. 

12. Now comes the point of Stridhan. Petitioner as defendant No.4 entered appearance in the suit by filing written statement wherein she categorically stated that the suit schedule land is the stridhan Property belonging to Charubala. Defendant No.1 also admitted in his written statement that Charubala was the original owner of the suit land by purchase. D.W.I in his deposition categorically said that the suit schedule property is the Stridhan property of Charubala. Plaintiff did not controvert the statement that the suit schedule land is the Stridhan property of Charubala in any manner, either in writing or oral evidence. As such the contention that the suit schedule land is the "Stridhan Property" of Charubala remains un-controverted and thus admitted. In reversing the findings of the trial Court that the suit land is the "Stridhan property" of, Chantbala, the lower appellate Court took the recourse of presumption by holding that it is presume that at the time of purchase of the Suit land Charubala was residing in her husband's house which led Further presumption of the lower appellate Court that Charubala purchased the suit land with the monetary help of her husband. Such presumption without any evidence, written or oral, adduced by the plaintiff-appellant-opposite party No.1 or in absence of any statement in the plaint or without any suggestion at the time of deposition has no legal basis and not sustainable in law. 

13. Considering the aforesaid facts and circumstances of the case, I find merit in this Rule and inclined to make the Rule absolute and as such the Rule is made absolute by setting aside the Judgment and decree dated 19-08-2004 and 26.08.2004 respectively passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Additional Court, Chittagong in Other Appeal No.132 of 2004; and upheld the judgment and decree dated 29.02.2004 and 06.03.2004 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, In-charge, Boalkhali Upazilla Court Chittagong in Other Suit No. 96 of 2001 decreeing the Suit in part in the preliminary form. 

14. The order of stay at the time of issuance of the Rule dated 12.03.2005 is hereby stand vacated. 

15. However, there will be no order as to cost. 

16. Send down the Lower Court's Record at once.

End.

full_judgment:
Mr. Mirza Hussain Haider, J.: This Ride Nisi was issued on an application filed by the petitioners under Article 102 Of the Constitution, calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned order dated 21.9.2003, passed by respondent No. 2, the learned Judge, Artha Rin Chittagong, in Artha Rin Suit No. 174 of 2003 (Annexure-G) should not be declared to be illegal, without lawful authority and is of no legal effect. 

2. The petitioner No. 1 is a limited company engaged in manufacturing and exporting readymade garments since its establishment. The petitioner No. 2 is the Managing Director of Petitioner No. 1. In course of their business and in order to manufacture and export the readymade garments the petitioners enjoy banking facilities from the respondent No, 4 bank and such facilities were increased, renewed and revised from time to time. The petitioners, in course of business, obtained a Master (Export) L/C amounting to US$ 63,960.00 and the same was processed through the respondent No. 4 bank and accordingly the petitioners were allowed to open back to back L/C for importation of raw materials. After utilization of the imported raw materials the petitioner exported the goods in part and the sale proceeds were realized against the export. Thereafter the residue of finished goods, amounting to US$ 32,848.20 was exported. by the petitioner and all the relevant documents were submitted to the respondent No. 4 to negotiate. Thereafter the petitioner No. 2 was informed by respondent No. 4.that the foreign bank had returned the full 'set of shipping documents relating to export bill No. LDE/ FDBC/ GMT/ 258198. for US$ 32,848.20 from Barclays Bank (PLC) London. But on scrutiny of the said documents the respondent No. 4 found that the first original bill of lading which was submitted. to the bank was missing. Accordingly the respondent No. 4 by its letter dated 01.03.2000 informed the petitioner that the respondent No. 4 is in continuous contact with the consignee's bank, i.e. Barclays Bank (PLC) London and shipping. company abroad to know the fate of 1/3 original bill of lading for US$ 32,848.20. However, the sale proceed was not repatriated. 

3. The petitioner No. 1 as plaintiff instituted a Money Suit No. 14 of 2002 impleading the respondent No. 4 and its officials and some other persons as defendants claiming compensation of TK. 2,96,42,400.00 against respondent No. 4 for the business loss caused clue to their negligence in the aforesaid consignment. The respondent No. 4 appeared in the said Money Suit and filed written statement denying material allegations of the plaint. The said suit is pending in the Court of Commercial Court-1 and Joint District Judge. Chittagong. 

4. During the pendency of the said suit the respondent No. 4 as plaintiff instituted Mortgage Suit No. 134 of 2003 before the respondent No. 2, the Artha Rin Adalat, Chittagong for realisation of money amounting to TK. 44,25,877. 22 by enforcing the mortgage on the- plea that the present petitioner failed to execute some portion of the export order and-- the documents submitted by the present petitioners through the plaintiff bank to sell the stock lot in United Kingdom were sent back by the same bank on the ground that the documents were discrepant and as such the petitioners are unable to pay the amount which -should be realized from the defendant petitioner. 

5. The petitioners filed written statement' in the said suit denying all material allegations of the plaint contending. inter alia, that due to the negligence of the respondent bank the petitioners incurred monetary loss to the extent of more than TK. 2,96,42,400.00 for which Money Suit No. 14 of 2002 has been filed against the respondent bank which has been renumbered as Suit No.15 of 2003. 

6. The instant suit filed by the respondent bank, subsequently, was renumbered as Artha Rin Suit No. 174 of 2003. Thereafter the defendant petitioner on 21.9.2003 filed an application under section 21 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 praying for holding settlement conference to settle the dispute between the parties by the alternative dispute resolution as contemplated in the said Ain. The said application was heard by the respondent No.2, the Artha Rin Adalat and the same was rejected on the plea that there is no unconditional consent from the plaintiff bank in holding such conference and thereby fixed 22.10.2003 for hearing of the case. 

7. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with order No. 12 dated 21.9.2003 the petitioners obtained the present Rule as aforesaid. 

8. Mr. Shah Md. Munir Sharif, the learned Advocate for the petitioners upon taking us through the writ petition along with the annexure submits that section 21 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 (hereinafter referred to as the said Ain) has been incorporated in Chapter-5 under the heading “বিকল্প পদ্ধতিতে বিরোধ নিষ্পত্তি” which contains sections 21 to 25. According to Mr. Sharif the language of the section 21 is very clear wherein it has been provided that after submission of the written statement, if the Court deems proper for holding settlement conference, then ask the parties, their engaged lawyers and their representatives to remain present in the said settlement conference to settle the dispute by such settlement. That means according to him the Court on perusal of the pleadings of both the parties will make such decision and in making such decision section 24 of the said Ain is also to be taken into consideration. In section 24 of the said Ain it has been said that the financial institution if agrees to resolve the dispute in the manner as provided in section 21 or 22 of the said Ain, then the Board of Directors of the said financial institution may delegate powers to the central, regional or local level competent officers for resolving the dispute and circulate the same to the concerned officers and to the concerned Artha Rin Adalat. Relying on the supplementary affidavit, which contains a copy of a circular being Nirdesh Biggapti No. 3586 dated 7.8.2003 from Head Office, 110, Motijheel C/A. Dhaka (Annexure-H) Mr., Sharif, submits that the consent has been given by the Bank and the power to settlement of dispute has also been given to certain officers for holding settlement conference or mediation/ arbitration as contemplated in sections 21 and 22 of the said Ain and thereby to take effective decision of settling the dispute by such' alternative procedure subject to the condition laid down in "annexure kha" Of the said Notification. The copy of the said circular has also been sent to all Artha Rin Adalats. This consent of the bank given in general by the Board of Directors to make fulfill the terms of settlement conference or mediation/ arbitration as the case may be, complete. Under such circumstances he submits that such consent having already been given by the financial institution/ bank, the observation as to 'unconditional consent of the bank is not there of the respondent No. 2, the Artha Rin Adalat, are erroneous and as such the same are without lawful authority. He submits that on this ground the Court cannot reject the petition rather such rejection has caused embargo in disposing of the matter by alternative procedure as contemplated in the new Ain. He then submits that section 21 is quite distinguishable with those of section 22. The consent of the bank is required as it appears from the proviso to section 22 (1). But there is no such condition in section 21 rather section 21 clearly specified that it is the Adalat who upon perusing the pleadings of both the parties will exercise its discretion to hold a settlement conference lo settle the dispute in an alternative manner. In the present case referring to the impugned order he submits that there is no reflection of perusing of the pleadings of both the parties and formation of mind of the learned Judge to invoke the provision of section 21 which is a process incorporated in the Ain for the purpose of resolving the dispute by alternative procedure and thereby save time and money of both the parties in recovering the unpaid loan. He submits that the learned judge did not exercise his discretion judiciously and as such the impugned order rejecting to hold settlement conference is without lawful authority. In this regard he submits that reliance can be made on the case of H.M.M. Alam Vs. Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and others, reported in 9 BLC (HC) 331. 

9. On the other hand Mr. S.M. Atikur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondent bank, at the very outset, on the face of the reasoning’s given in the impugned order, could not agree with the same. He admits that sections 21 and 22 are quite distinguishable from each other, though in both the sections, alternative remedy for settling the dispute has been incorporated by the present Ain. Referring section 22(i), Mr. Rahman could not build up his argument .to controvert those of Mr. Shard supported by the aforesaid decision. Upon reading the languages used in the provisions of law Mr. Rahman also admitted that section 22 requires consent of the financial institution but in section 21 there is no such express provision in the law. He next tried to impress upon this court by submitting that the Annexure-H which has been filed by the learned Advocate for the petitioners along with the supplementary affidavit, is a general direction to all the officers of the bank. But such direction is subject to the terms and conditions incorporated in the schedule annexed to such direction circulated through Nirdesh Biggapti, circular. He submits that the petitioners cannot take advantage of such direction issued by the respondent bank unless the terms and conditions incorporated therein are fulfilled. However, since he could not develop his submission on the face of the reasoning’s used in the impugned order, he left the matter upon the Court for decision. 

10. We have perused the writ petition along with the appended papers and also the relevant law and decision cited by the petitioners. To resolve the point raised before this Court, we are to see the intention of the legislature in incorporating the provision of section 21 in Chapter -5 under the heading “বিকল্প পদ্ধতিতে বিরোধ নিষ্পত্তি” Therein it appears that section 21 provided for resolving the dispute by holding settlement conference. The sub sections to section 21 deals with the procedure of holding such conference. The main provision has been incorporated in sub section (1) of section 21 which reads as follows: 
“21(1): চতুর্থ পরিচ্ছেদে বর্ণিত সাধারণ পদ্ধতিতে মামলার বিচার বা শুনানী সম্পর্কিত যে বিধানই থাকুক না কেন, এই আইনের অধীন দায়েরকৃত কোন মামলায় বিবাদী কর্তৃক লিখিত জবাব দাখিলের পর, আদালত, ধারা ২৪ এর বিধান সাপেক্ষে, যথাযথ মনে করিলে পরবর্তী কাযক্রম স্থগিত রাখিয়া একটি মীমাংসা সভা আহ্বান করিতে পারিবে এবং উক্ত সভায় পক্ষগণ, তাহাদের নিযুক্ত আইনজীবি ও প্রতিনিধিগণকে উপস্থিত থাকিতে নির্দেশ প্রদান করিতে পারিবে।”
The other provisions of section 21 not required to be considered for the purpose of disposal of this Rule hence the same are not referred to similarly section 22 deals with mediation arbitration. Proviso to section 22 (1) is required to be looked onto for the purpose of this Rule which reads as follows
“২২। তবে শর্ত থাকে যে, পক্ষগণ যদি এই মর্মে আদালতের নিকট দরখাস্ত করিয়া আবেদন করেন যে, তাহারা মধ্যস্থতার মাধ্যমে মামলা নিষ্পত্তি করিতে আগ্রহী, তাহা হইলে এই ধারার অধীন মধ্যস্থতার মাধ্যমে নিষ্পত্তির চেষ্টার জন্য মামলা প্রেরন করা আদালতের জন্য্ বাধ্যতামূলক হইবে।
The other sub sections 22 deals with the procedure - to hold such mediation or arbitration. Section 23 deals with limitation/ restriction on the alternative procedure for settling the dispute which reads as follows:

Upon going through the aforesaid provisions of chapter-5 for alternative dispute resolution as contemplated in the present law it appears that these provisions have been incorporated in the new law for the purpose of resolving the dispute by alternative procedure thinking just to save time, energy and money of both the parties in settling the dispute by understanding between them. 

11. On a comparative study of the provisions of section 21 and 22 it appears that both the process can be invoked after the written statement is filed by the defendant and subject to the provision of section 24, the proceeding of the suit would pend and any of the procedures for settlement of the dispute can be invoked. The only difference we find in the two provisions as to “আদালত যথাযথ মনে করিলে” in section 21 and the proviso of section 22(i) which clearly provided that in case the parties make' an application to the Adalat for mediation / arbitration expressing its/their eagerness about the same then it would compel the Adalat to send the matter for mediation/ arbitration. That means there is no such compulsion in section 21. So this can be said that the provision and procedure of section 22 is different from those of section 21. From reading section 21 it appears that if the Court deems fit and proper after filing and perusing the written statement then the Court can invoke the provision of this section. But section 22 clearly said that if the parties desires then the Court has no other choice but to go for mediation arbitration. Reading section 21 we find that the power given to the Court under section 21 is a discretionary power to be exercised judiciously. In this respect it will not be out of place to mention that the learned judge confused itself by mixing the provisions of section 21 and 22. 

12. The impugned order which has been challenged in this writ petition is a very short order, which reads as follows: 
“বাদী হাজিরা দিয়াছে। বিবাদীপক্ষ ২১ এর ধারামতে একখানা দরখাস্ত দাখিল করিয়া মিমাংসা সভার প্রার্থনা করিয়াছে। কপি দিয়াছে শুনিলাম। বাদী ব্যাংকের শর্তহীন সম্মতি না থাকায় প্রার্থনা না মঞ্জুর করা গেল। মামলা শুনানীর জন্য পক্ষগণকে প্রস্তুত হইতে নির্দেশ দেওয়া গেল (ভি ও পি) বিবাদীপক্ষ আর একখানা দরখাস্ত দাখিল করিয়া সময়ের প্রার্থনা করিয়াছে। শুনিলাল। প্রার্থনা মঞ্জুর করা গেল। (ভি ও পি) আগামী ২২/১০/২০০৩ ইং তাং পি, এইচ।”
So it appears from the impugned order that the reasons which have been shown in the said order while rejecting the prayer is “বাদী ব্যাংকের শর্তহীন সম্মতি না থাকায় প্রার্থনা না মঞ্জুর করা গেল”। It also appears that a certified copy of the application has been annexed with writ petition as Annexure 'F'. It appears from the said application that a copy of the same has been served upon the learned Advocate for the bank and the learned advocate while receiving the said copy did not endorse any objection therein in this regard. So we do not understand as to how the learned Judge could come to a conclusion that there is no unconditional consent to that effect? 

13. We have already stated earlier that the power given in section 21 is a discretionary power. Holding of settlement conference does not depend on the whims of either party. It is the satisfaction of the Court and if the Court on perusal of the pleadings of the parties deems fit and proper to hold settlement conference then only the section can be invoked. The prime consideration of section 21 is the satisfaction of the Court whether the pleadings show that the dispute may be resolved by settlement conference. But there being no such satisfaction or dissatisfaction reflected in the impugned order passed by the learned Judge in the order sheet we do not find that the impugned order has been passed in accordance with law. Mere consent of the bank or either party is not the subject matter for consideration in dealing with the case under section - 21 of the Ain. So the reasons given in the impugned order is uncalled for and the same is without lawful authority.

14. Though section 21 does not require for any application to be filed for holding such settlement conference but even then there is no restriction of filing application by either of the parties which would be nothing but drawing the Court's attention in the matter that on perusal of the pleadings the matter can be disposed of by alternative dispute resolution in the manner incorporated in section 21. Had it been a question of mediation or arbitration as incorporated in section 22 of the Ain and had it been initiated by an application filed by the parties then the proviso of section-22 would be invoked and the court would be compelled to refer the matter for such settlement. But in section 21 it is not necessary. The prime thing is, as we have stated, earlier, that the Court should deem fit and proper to refer the matter for settlement conference.

ক) মীমাংসার তারিখ পর্যন্ত সুদ হিসাব করিয়া Cost of Fund কভার করিয়া এবং শাখার আর খাত প্রভিশন বিকলন না করিয়া যে পরিমান সুদ ব্যাংকিং নীতিমালার মওকুফ করা যায় সেই পরিমান সুদ মওকুফের সুযোগ দেওয়া যাইতে পারে ৷

17. Accordingly, it appears that different officials have been given their limitations/ authority, to deal with such mediation/ settlement conference, the conditions for coming to settlement and the ambit of settlement. 'Reading Annexure H, copy of which has already been circulated to all the concerned banks and the Artha Rin Adalats, we are, of the view that it is the general consent given by the Board of Director of the respondent bank to hold, settlement conference, mediation/arbitration and resolve the dispute by alternative dispute resolution without unnecessarily spending time, energy and money in litigations. In this respect if we look into the preamble of the Ain we will find that the whole purpose of the same is to realize the unpaid loan given by the financial institution to the borrower for different purposes of their business/ commerce/ trade. The preamble of the Ain reads as follows:  
“যেহেতু আর্থিক প্রতিষ্ঠান কতৃর্কি প্রদত্ত ঋণ আদায়ের জন্য প্রচলিত অইিনের অধিকতঃ সংশোধন ও সংহতকৱণ প্রয়োজনীয়, সেহেতু এতদদ্বারা নিম্নরূপ আইন করা হইলঃ”
So, the legislature while incorporating the Ain has given prime consideration for realization of the unpaid loan. Again it will not be out of place & mention that it has become a trend and culture on the part of the borrowers of the bank of not paying back the money within the time as specified. This culture has developed in this country for many years and probably keeping this trend of proposition in the mind the legislature has been compelled to incorporate such law. However, if we see the purpose of incorporated such Ain we will be able to come to a conclusion that for the purpose of realizing the unpaid money from the borrowers of the bank this Ain has been enacted. Since the whole purpose of enacting the law is for recovery of loan and as such the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 has been incorporation upon consolidating the existing law of 1990, which was firstly enacted in 1990 and Since under the existing law it appeared that by filing suits or execution cases money could be recovered but not in a short span of time, the legislature has incorporated the provision of chapter 5 in the new Ain for easy recovery of money within a short time and as such alternative dispute resolution has been incorporated in the new Ain for the purpose of realizing money without spending much time and money in litigations. As such chapter 5 has been incorporated in the, present Ain allowing the parties to ask for amicable settlement under section 22 and /or under section 21 the Adalat can invoke it if it is deemed fit and proper on perusal of the pleadings of both the parties. 
For the reasons and discussions made hereinabove and also the relevant law and the decision cited by the petitioners, we are of the view that this Rule has merit and thus, the Rule is made absolute. The order which has been complained of is hereby declared to be illegal, without lawful authority and is of no legal effect. 

18. The learned Judge, Artha Rin Adalat, First Court, Chittagong is directed to convene a settlement conference if he so deems fit and proper on perusal of the pleadings of the parties. 

19. However, there will be no order as to costs. 

	End.
